maintopic: O.E.E.C.-REPORT FROM CANADIAN DELEGATION TO ECONOMIC POLICY COMMITTEE

speechtext:
Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of
Finance): Mr. Speaker, I have now received a report from the Canadian delegation to the economic policy committee of the O.E.E.C. which met in Paris on April 18 and 19. I should like to inform the house of several important developments which took place at these meetings.
Hon. members will be interested to know that the economic policy committee, composed of senior officials from all the member countries, is expected to become one of the principal organs of the new O.E.C.D. designed to promote closer international cooperation and consultation over the whole field of economic policy both national and international. Because this was the first meeting of the economic policy committee since ratification of the O.E.C.D. convention by Canada and the United States, considerable attention was devoted to plans for the future work of the organization for promoting closer economic collaboration among the member countries. The work of this committee is of particular significance to Canada because its membership now embraces all the principal countries of western Europe, the United Kingdom and the United States, which together account for a very high proportion of Canada's total foreign trade.
In addition to making plans for its future work, the economic policy committee on this occasion reviewed the current economic situation and future prospects of member countries particularly as they affected the trade and financial relationships among them.
With a view to extending and intensifying the work of the O.E.C.D. the committee decided to establish two working groups to study and consult upon problems of economic policy where such action seemed particularly timely and likely to produce the most valuable results. The first group will deal with problems of economic growth. The second group will deal with the balance of payments and the monetary, fiscal and other related policies. Canada will be represented on both
working groups. The economic policy committee expects to receive reports from these two groups within the next few months with a view to making proposals for action to the ministerial council of the O.E.C.D. later in the year.
I should like now to table the terms of reference for the two working groups established by the economic policy committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: O.E.E.C.-REPORT FROM CANADIAN DELEGATION TO ECONOMIC POLICY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think all hon. members will have learned with satisfaction that some encouraging progress is being made in the work of the economic policy group in laying the foundation for the transformation of the O.E.E.C. into the organization for European co-operation and development which could be one of the most important agencies in the development of Atlantic economic co-operation. We can only hope that the encouraging progress that has been begun in the work of the economic policy committee will be continued in the meetings of the subcommittees and the meetings of the full committee to which the minister referred.

maintopic: O.E.E.C.-REPORT FROM CANADIAN DELEGATION TO ECONOMIC POLICY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, from the standpoint of Canada I think it is a good thing that the O.E.C.D. has set up these two committees and has this work now under way. From the standpoint of our country I think both committees can be of importance, the one having to do with growth, of which we do not have too much at this time, and the other having to do with the balance of payments, which is a difficult problem for Canada even now and in the case of Europe is of very great importance. I think for Canada this is a matter of urgency, and we hope that the O.E.C.D. in the future will bring about freer trade within the Atlantic area and will make it possible for Canada to resume adequate growth within our nation.

Mr. Speaker, on the point of order, the hon. member for Essex East just insists on making himself more and more absurd the further he goes in this matter. He has read a portion of the citation, Mr. Speaker, and then has beclouded the whole issue with a mass of verbiage. Let me read the citation in full for the instruction of the hon. member. Citation 186 reads as follows:
(1)	There are only two ways In which a question can be withdrawn from the order paper: first, by a written notice, by the member putting the question, to the Clerk of the house, and, secondly, by the member, in his place in the house, informing the Speaker that he desires the question to be dropped.
(2)	Oral notices for future proceedings do not exist in the Canadian House of Commons. It is useless for a member to say: "Mr. Speaker, I give notice that I will move a certain question tomorrow." This would not give him any precedence on the next day and he would not thereby acquire the right to speak on matters not standing on the order paper. An exception must be made in respect of certain routine proceedings dealing with the observance of proprieties of the house, the maintenance of its authority, the conduct of its officers, the management of its business, the correctness of its records or any other similar matter brought up by the Prime Minister and settled without the passage of any resolution. A minister may also announce from his seat that he will later make an official statement on some important matter but he does so as a courtesy to the members. These indications of the government's intentions are not the kind of notices required under standing order 41 which must be printed in the Votes and Proceedings.
The authority of the house is not an issue here. This does not arise out of any statement or matter brought up by the Prime Minister. It does not relate to the conduct of any officer of the house or the management of the business of the house, or the correctness of the records of the house, or any other similar matter, brought up by the Prime Minister and settled without the passage of any resolution.
With great respect, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Essex East has been in the house a long time and some of us who have some regard for him do not like to see him making himself look so utterly absurd as he is insisting on doing today.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word on the point of order, particularly about the many precedents there are with respect to the very procedure which the hon. member for Essex East has adopted on this occasion. There is no difference in principle, as I am sure Your Honour will agree, between getting up and putting, as is done practically every day on the orders of the day, a question to a minister and asking him to take it as notice, and doing what my hon. friend from Essex East has done today. All he has done is to say that with respect to a matter that would not appear on the order paper at all, namely the reference of a document to a committee, that as a matter of routine proceedings he intends on a future occasion to take that action. Of course hon. members who are chairmen of committees are constantly making similar motions with respect to concurrence in reports of committees, and they get up at this stage of the proceedings and give notice that they intend to do that on a future occasion.
Of course we all recognize that if the hon. member for Essex East was trying to place something on the order paper which would give him precedence over some other hon. member, that would be an improper thing to do, because there is a precedence laid down in the regular standing orders of the house. But in routine proceedings there is no precedence. Whichever hon. members catches your eye first, be it the Prime Minister, the chairman of a committee, the whip seeking to change the membership of a committee, this is accepted by the Chair in the order in which it happens. All the hon. member for Essex East was doing was seeking to give the house advance warning of what he proposes to do in order that the house might exercise its jurisdiction and supervision over a body with respect to which the Minister of Finance disclaims any responsibility, and proclaims there is a parliamentary responsibility.

Mr. Speaker, last etening in the three minutes at my disposal I made reference to the good work of the minister and his officials and to the failure of world leaders to seize opportunities to promote world peace between world wars I and II and since.
Our unanimous support of democratic principles and parliamentary institutions, our common objective which is the promotion of world peace, are, I know, taken for granted, and on that basis we all participate in this debate. While we may differ as to the pathway to peace and as to the meaning of current events, we all seek a single objective and welcome this opportunity to present our views with conviction as members of a free parliament.
The members of this group believe that the present circumstances present an opportunity and a particular challenge to Canada to

External Affairs
utilize its pool of good will that exists throughout the world in taking a friendly but strong, independent and constructive approach to the tangled skein of world problems. In that connection, on behalf of this group 1 should like to urge the Prime Minister to speak with the same clear voice and to represent the views of the people of Canada on these world questions as he did at the recent prime ministers' conference.
In the struggle between the democratic and totalitarian forms of government Canada cannot remain neutral. We must always stand squarely on the side of freedom and with the genuine forces of freedom. However, let me point out that the nature of this struggle is constantly changing. Revolutionary developments in weapons have underlined the danger and absurdity of relying on military strength as the chief method of settling international disputes, even though in some cases it is considered to be the only method. It is increasingly evident that the traditional policy of accumulating arms diverts us from channels of action through which purely effective policies can be pursued. These developments require new departures in Canada's contribution to the emerging world community.
The C.C.F. party believes that Canada's foreign and defence policies must be reappraised and reshaped if we are to play an effective part in the world's search for peace, and particularly in view of the blunders that have been committed by the United States in recent years in the field of foreign policy. It is because of these blunders and errors, this lack of judgment in United States foreign policy, that we emphasize the need for Canada not to remain silent on these occasions, but to speak with a stronger and clearer voice.
These blunders are causing concern to many Canadians and to people throughout the world. As a matter of fact, from correspondence I have received from a wide section of the community, people who support all parties in the house, and from organizations and from meetings I have attended I gather that this criticism is growing, and there is a greater and greater demand that Canada should utilize the pool of good will toward us that exists throughout the world and speak more firmly and clearly on some of these questions.
In our opinion, Mr. Speaker, the United States government, despite its announced concern for the rights of the people and its contention that it has not forgotten its revolutionary birth, has consistently supported reactionary and right wing governments throughout the world, and no one can deny

that. I am paraphrasing conversations I have had and correspondence and resolutions I have received.
At the beginning the United States government was of the opinion that President Sukarno of Indonesia did not have the support of his people. Events have proven that the United States government was in error, and only a few days ago President Sukarno of Indonesia conferred with the President of the United States. I am mentioning a few of these blunders and errors in judgment which have had serious consequences in the world in recent years.
Let me also say that the government of the United States supported Syngman Rhee with massive financial and military contributions. Events proved that he was one of the nastiest fascists going until he was driven from office by a popular uprising, over which United States policy had no control, with apparently little forewarning.
The same story can be told with respect to Turkey, where liberal thinkers and students were murdered by the reactionary government of Menderes which was supported by the United States. In Laos the United States government proved again that they could not leave well enough alone and, no doubt acting under Dulles' precept that neutralism was immoral, started subverting the 1954 Geneva agreement with a view to installing a right wing government in Laos. This plot backfired when the communists inevitably gave support to their own people and a civil war ensued.
Britain has now had to come to the rescue of the United States government to arrange a cease fire, as has happened before. Undoubtedly any government that will be set up in the future in Laos will be more pro-communist than the one which existed a year ago, until United States government intervention led to the installation of a right wing government. Only today there is word from the United Nations that the President of the United States is calling into conference the leaders of both houses to deal with further difficulties that have developed because of this blunder in United States policy in recent days.
In South Viet Nam things are no better, Mr. Speaker. Some people make much of the fact that President Diem is a professed Christian. He is a funny sort of Christian from my point of view. I have talked to quite a few representatives from Southeast Asia, and I believe he is a vulgar fascist who rigs elections as well as, or better than, any communist. According to the news from this area in recent days his days of rule are numbered in Viet Nam because he does not

represent the legitimate wishes of a people seeking freedom and a democratic form of government.
Then in Saudi Arabia the monstrous Ibn Saud rules with mediaeval splendour amongst his slaves and harem, fully supported by a United States government which places the profits of the big oil companies far, far ahead of the rights of man in that area.
Then there was the unfortunate U-2 flight which occurred after the meeting of President Eisenhower with Mr. Khrushchev and which further increased world tension, suspicion, and Mr. Khrushchev's difficulties with China. On Tuesday last I spent a very interesting hour or two with a very important individual, a highly respected gentleman with great knowledge, great understanding and experience. I refer to Right Hon. Philip Noel-Baker. He was telling me about developments in these areas and of his conviction that Mr. Khrushchev wants to develop a policy of co-operation with western governments, a system to curtail armaments and to ease tension. He is opposed by the government of China in this respect, and this unfortunate U-2 flight undermined his influence with some of his own people and made particularly difficult his discussions at this crucial time with representatives of the government of mainland China.
Finally, the latest and most flagrant example of blundering has been the support by the United States government of the counter-revolutionary invasion in Cuba. Canadian opinion in this respect is well reflected in our press today. I should like to quote a few of the headlines:
Kennedy Endorses Efforts of Invaders-Globe and Mail, April 19, 1961.
The Cuban Tragedy-Globe and Mail. April 21, 1961.
Kennedy Claims TJ.S. Right to Intervention in Cuba-Gazette, April 21, 1961.
U.N. Aghast at Kennedy's Blundering in Cuba- Globe and Mail, April 21, 1961.
Kennedy Doctrine Applies to Canada-U.S. Sets Itself Judge of Action to be Taken if Red Threat Rises-Globe and Mail, April 22, 1961.
U.S. Top Brass Backed Rebels' Plans-Gazette, April 22, 1961.
Global Scales Tipping Against U.S.-Globe and Mail, April 27, 1961.
Arab Suspicions of U.S. Intensified-Globe and Mail, April 27, 1961.
The minister, when he was speaking, said we must stand by our friends. On behalf of this group-I am speaking for the C.C.F. group this afternoon, and I have their unanimous support and endorsation-let me say that the C.C.F. wants to be friendly with everybody, but our principle should be to stand by what is right first. Speaking on behalf of this group I should like to deal briefly with some aspects of international affairs, and other C.C.F. speakers, if they
External Affairs
have the opportunity, will further develop the theme I advance in the limited time at my disposal.
We believe that because of United States blundering in foreign policy in so many areas, the thing for Canada to do is to take a friendly-you can have differences amongst friends-constructive approach to world problems and not to remain silent when those things concern Canadians and threaten world peace, and in so doing give leadership. A large number of nations have a great deal of respect for Canada. This is evident to anyone who travels in Europe or Asia. Canada is highly respected throughout the world. Canada is in a position to use influence to give leadership, and particularly moral suasion.
Now, Mr. Speaker, with respect to disarmament and nuclear tests I should like to say, first of all, that we are glad to give the minister full credit for all his ceaseless, untiring efforts to promote disarmament and the cessation of nuclear tests. I am sure of this, that if it were left to our Secretary of State for External Affairs it would not be long before we would have some sort of agreement. His efforts in this respect have earned the appreciation and gratitude of all Canadians. I hear that stated on all sides, and I have no hesitation in repeating it. Canadians who are mightily concerned about world peace, not forgetting that courageous little group known as the Voice of Women, which I am glad to note has had the blessing of the Prime Minister, have expressed this point of view with regard to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
In our opinion Canada should continue to support and demand an immediate ban on nuclear tests, both to avoid the hazards of fall-out and as a first step toward nuclear disarmament. We should propose a treaty to establish a non-nuclear club of nations pledged not to manufacture, store, or permit nuclear weapons on their soil, or to use such weapons at any time. In the nuclear age effective disarmament has become a condition of survival. Canada must play a much more dynamic role in the promotion of universal disarmament. To assist in this task a special branch should be established in the Department of External Affairs, adequately staffed by nuclear scientists and other experts for continuous study of the problems involved. We recognize that these problems are involved and complicated.
The minister has frequently said that war is international suicide, and we agree with him wholeheartedly. However, some United States generals do not agree with us, you know, and have suggested that such a statement is an exaggeration of the facts. In their

External Affairs
opinion, in the event of a nuclear war, casualties in the United States would not exceed between 30 million and 50 million.
A few days ago I had a most interesting conversation, as I said before, with Right Hon. Philip Noel-Baker, whose integrity and veracity is unquestioned. We discussed the growing burden of armaments on all mankind. I think all persons will pay tribute to the great work this gentleman has done throughout the years as a member of parliament of Great Britain, for many years a member of the Labour cabinet, as a Nobel prize winner, as a member of various important international committees, and as a member of the Society of Friends.
This is a burden that is increasing from day to day. Total world defence expenditures in 1960 came to $110 billion. Those are all that can really be assessed. In 1914 there were 4 million men under arms, whereas in 1960 there were 16 million men under arms. We are not sure if that figure is accurate; it may be an underestimate. The expenditure on military research in the United States in 1960 came to $8.4 billion. The expenditure on military research in Canada for this year is nearly $45 million. Military research; what does it means? It means research into improving the weapons of war, the weapons of destruction. Military research has helped to bring the arms race to the point of frenzy; indeed, it is the arms race in its most dangerous form.
Therefore we urge every effort to reach an agreement that will provide adequate inspection and include all important states, and that will also prohibit all forms of military research and development with the testing of new weapons and training in their use. If only military research were ended and the world scientists with their present funds and equipment diverted to peaceful projects, there is no limit to the benefits which they might bring to mankind and which mankind throughout the whole world is earnestly seeking.
I now have a few words to say about NORAD and NATO. Yesterday the minister quoted from the memorandum of the Canadian Labour Congress to the government of Canada this year with what I took to be a certain degree of relish. However, let me say this. While there may appear to be some varying opinions as to the application of our socialist principles to international affairs, let me inform the minister they simply arise from minor differences in the assessment of the present situation and as to certain facts. I am sure that he and many others will be surprised with the unity of principles, policy and purpose that will be demonstrated by

the progressive democratic political forces in Canada in the very near days ahead.

I wish to say a word or two with respect to NORAD. The revolution in weapons technology makes two facts obvious to reasonable men. The first is that annihilation is now a physical possibility. The second is that there is no direct defence against nuclear missiles. Therefore in our opinion policy must be based on these realities. Canada should cease wasteful expenditure on obsolete weapons. NORAD was intended to meet the threat of manned bombers. In the age of missiles, it is obsolete. Therefore in our opinion the NORAD agreements should be terminated.
Canada must make a general and searching reappraisal of its defence role. We should institute a major reduction in defence expenditures as a first step toward peace and to release funds urgently needed for economic aid abroad and social progress at home. Just think of these facts, Mr. Speaker. The direct costs of NORAD in 1961-62-that is this fiscal year-will be $182,127,000. The direct costs of NATO in this fiscal year 1961-62 will be $455,545,000. They have been going up increasingly since the establishment of NATO. Just compare those figures with that of nearly 700,000 unemployed. We in the C.C.F. unhesitatingly say that we believe these large sums can be more fruitfully spent in providing employment at home and assistance to underdeveloped nations abroad.
I now wish to say a few words with respect to NATO. NATO has played its part in the maintenance of western European security. However, it has concentrated on a military role and has failed to adapt its policies to the growing importance of the economic and social front in the present world struggle. We believe that the extension of nuclear weapons to any further states and organizations threatens disaster to the world. We therefore oppose Canadian troops being supplied with such weapons at home or abroad.
My time is limited, Mr. Speaker. The leader of this group has placed on the record the C.C.F. position with respect to NATO. It
can

be found in Hansard for March 28, 1961, at pages 3443-3444. As I said, my time is too limited to permit recapitulation of this policy and the reasons for it. Suffice it for me to say at this time that this policy was adopted at the C.C.F. national convention held in Regina in 1960, and is supported by the British Columbia federation of labour, the Vancouver labour council, nearly all unions in British Columbia whether they are in the labour congress or outside it, and by dozens and dozens of local unions across Canada that have written to our office expressing their support.
I now want to say a few words with respect to Cuba. Without a doubt many Canadians are disturbed with recent events in Cuba and the policy of the United States government. This concern is reflected in editorials in numerous Canadian newspapers. To illustrate this concern I quote from three of them. First, the Vancouver Province, which normally supports the Progressive Conservatives, in April, 1961 had this to say. I quote only briefly because of lack of time. The editorial is headed "A Continent of Cubas" and reads in part as follows:
A most disturbing aspect of the Cuban crisis is its further development of a pattern already apparent in most South American nations.
The Castro revolution was neither a freak of chance nor a malignant communist plot. It was the logical outcome of the conditions that created it.
And again:
The misery of the masses and the corruption of the government (are) surely producing a revolution.
As in Cuba, the communists are confidently standing by ready to aid, assist and guide the revolutions when they come. And undoubtedly to assist in triggering them when the time is ripe.
But the revolutions are not made in Russia. They are home grown.
And unless the western world can find some effective and speedy method of achieving peaceful and friendly revolutions there, we are likely to find a continent of Cubas on our doorstep.

I could quote from other editorials all across Canada and in Great Britain but time will not permit my doing so. Serious concern is also being expressed in Great Britain, and British Labour party members are suggesting that an inquiry into all aspects of the counterrevolutionary attack on Cuba should be undertaken by the United Nations. Canadians are very concerned. We strongly urge the government first to protest to the United States against its policies with respect to the recent counter-revolutionary attack on Cuba; second, to express complete disagreement with President Kennedy's interpretation of the Monroe doctrine as permitting direct intervention by the United States in the affairs of another state; third, to urge the use of the facilities of the United Nations and the co-operation of the organization of American states to assist in the development of a stable Cuban economy and the promotion of democratic and free, parliamentary institutions in that country.

The final sentence is:
The general assembly exhorts all member states to take such peaceful action as is open to them to remove existing tension.
In this field, again, we urge Canada to use its good offices and good will in the peaceful ways suggested to bring this situation to a satisfactory conclusion.
The minister mentioned the Columbia treaty. I have not time to deal with that now; therefore I will have to deal with the minister's comments under an appropriate item of the estimates of his department.
Before concluding I want to say a word or two about the commonwealth. The stand condemning racism taken recently by the commonwealth increases opportunities for enlarging the role of this unique association of peoples. We have no hesitation in saying that the members of this group are great supporters of the commonwealth and of the greater role it could play in the days ahead in working for world peace. The multiracial and geographically dispersed character of the commonwealth fits it ideally for the role of increasing co-operation among divergent parts of the world, thus reducing the dangerous effects of the cold war.
Therefore we say that Canada should support ever more effective consultation among the members of the commonwealth, both within and without the United Nations, and In so doing provide a strong and united moral force which could be very effective, we believe, in promoting the efforts toward world peace.
The minister mentioned that the United Nations is the world's most important organization. We agi-ee with him. The minister said that without the United Nations civilization would soon revert to savagery. We agree with those words also. It is because of this appreciation of the United Nations throughout the years that this group has emphasized the need for Canada to focus its civilian and military efforts on the general assembly and the agencies of the United Nations.
The United Nations represents the hope of progress toward a durable peace for all as the only existing, nearly universal, instrument of international conciliation. The C.C.F. again pledges its full support to every measure designed to enhance the prestige, authority and jurisdiction of the United Nations and all its agencies. Canada is obligated under the United Nations charter-
-to make available ... armed forces, assistance and facilities ... for the purpose of maintaining international peace and security.
In our opinion it is time for us, in concert with other middle and smaller powers, to insist that the general assembly find ways to create a permanent international police force.
[Mr. Herridge.l
Canada should immediately create a well-equipped mobile force at the call of the United Nations.
The United Nations agencies, in our opinion, should form the major channel for providing international economic aid. This is important both to strengthen the world organization and because it would avoid placing recipient nations under an obligation to a single power. Some nations do not like being obliged to another nation. The immensely increased aid program which the C.C.F. proposes should therefore be directed accordingly.
Canada should base its votes in the United Nations on the merits of the issues rather than, as it has done on occasion in the past, particularly in some years, on bloc alignments.
It is obvious that the United Nations cannot be truly effective so long as a major world power is denied membership. We believe Canada should recognize the People's Republic of China and support its admission to the United Nations. Recognition does not involve approval of China's system of government. We have said that repeatedly. However, a non-recognition which seeks to isolate China adds to world tensions, makes the settlement of major international issues, such as disarmament, difficult if not impossible, and is totally lacking in a sense of reality. We should not shirk the difficulties when we have to do something like this. We have to start to blaze the trail in this direction.
The C.C.F. welcomes the addition of many new nations to the councils of the United Nations and warmly congratulates their peoples on their freedom from foreign rule. By economic aid, appropriate trade policies and increasingly closer relations within and without the United Nations, Canada should support their independence, integrity, sovereign rights and growth.
We realize the great difficulties which face any person in the position of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He has our sympathy and our support, and we wish him well in all he undertakes for the welfare of the people of Canada and all he endeavours to accomplish in order to bring about a goal that looks somewhat distant at the present time, but a goal we must continue striving for, that of universal world peace.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, we urge the Canadian government to accept its full responsibility; to accept the unique challenge offered today-and it is unique because of our position and our moral force in the world -to give leadership to all those nations that hold Canada with affection, in great respect

and high regard, and who seek some guidance from us, to march with us along the road to peace.

Mr. Speaker, in following the eloquent hon. member for Kootenay West I should first like to say that the good wishes he expressed on behalf of his group to the distinguished Secretary of State for External Affairs are shared, I think, by all hon. members of the House of Commons.
As the Secretary of State for External Affairs spoke yesterday I was impressed by the fact that in many different fields the minister himself has made a very important and useful contribution. He has been an excellent spokesman for Canada, an inspiring leader at the United Nations, where I have had the privilege of observing him at work, and an initiator of policy. This afternoon I hope to persuade him and the hon. members of the house that this is a good time for Canada to make economic aid to the less rapidly developing countries the major initiative of Canadian foreign policy.
I know that determining Canadian foreign policy, political, economic and military, is an extremely complex matter. Certainly there are few things more difficult than deciding how our country should play its part as a member of the western defence alliance. Since our very survival is bound up with this question, our very best efforts must be devoted to building up the right kind of deterrent forces to prevent war. Many responsible persons believe that the arms race increases, rather than decreases, the chances of war breaking out. Then we all know that making weapons is a terrible waste of resources.
At the United Nations General Assembly last fall the Prime Minister of New Zealand said that 11 per cent of the productive capacities of the world are being used to produce armaments. For these and other reasons I think it was right for Canada to make disarmament one of its main objects at the recent session of the United Nations general assembly.
Many proposals were put forward, but none of them will have any effect unless the major powers are prepared to sit down and negotiate. Much as I would like to be optimistic about the possibilities of serious negotiations in the near future, I must say that the facts of life do not support optimism in this regard. I do not think there is going to be any serious negotiation on disarmament for some little time. Certainly nobody can take any satisfaction from the fact that it has been agreed that the subject of disarmament will be discussed in the early stages of the sixteenth assembly, because in that period millions of dollars will 90205-6-256i
External Affairs
be spent in all parts of the world producing things which have no purpose other than to destroy people and resources.
I recommend that economic aid to less developed countries should be Canada's major initiative in the 1960's for the following reasons. We are not one of the main military powers and because of this, in world politics, our role must be one of an ally, an intermediary, and from time to time a spokesman for Canada and other middle powers. This has been said very often.
Canada does not have the reputation anywhere of wanting the territory of other countries for military bases or for any other purpose. I do not think there is very much anti-Canadian feeling in the areas where our aid projects have been carried out. In the uncommitted countries I am informed there is a tendency for people to look at aid from the United States or the Soviet union as having a political objective.
The next reason is that we should do what we can, and I think there is great potential in Canada in this purpose, to stamp out some of the causes of war, and I refer to the unrest and dissatisfaction that grow among people who are hungry, ill-housed and illiterate. To this I would join the reason that we should help these people on humanitarian grounds.
In January of this year I was in Hong Kong, and I think most hon. members would come close to weeping if they saw the condition of thousands of refugees in that city. In that splendid book "To Plough with Hope", Donald Faris tells us something about the distribution of food in the world. He points out that about 60 per cent of the world's population is living on a near-starvation diet. That is less than 2,200 calories per person per day. These people, if placed side by side two feet apart, would circle the world 25 times. To get an idea of the size of this population I would suggest the following: to pass them in an automobile, if they were standing two feet apart in this manner, would take three and a half years driving 10 hours a day at the rate of 50 miles per hour.
Another argument is that raising living standards in the less developed parts of the world will provide greater markets for Canadian goods. This point, among others in this connection, has been made in the House of Commons on another occasion by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell). Instead of fighting to get a larger piece of the existing trade pie, why not do something to increase the size of the pie?
While the phrase may sound somewhat empty, I think an expansion of Canada's economic aid program would give us a chance to strike a blow for freedom and for free institutions. Let us do something to show

Mr. Speaker, I can see that the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency did not listen to my remarks, because I clearly said "during the six weeks I attended the proceedings", and, if I remember correctly, the hon. member arrived in New York one or two days before I left.
Mr. Speaker, that six-week period I was able to realize all the good the United Nations has accomplished in the 15 years it has existed.
I was also able to realize the splendid work that the countries which have inherited from Providence a higher civilization, a prosperous economy and an almost unlimited wealth have done in their efforts to promote peace.
I also saw the great spirit of understanding and fraternity of most of the delegates, and particularly those from western countries and Latin America. That spirit was reflected in a special way during the proceedings of the general assembly in 1959, under the distinguished chairmanship of Mr. Victor Be-launde from Peru. At the end of the session Mr. Belaunde said the assembly had been an assembly of peace. I feel it is proper to remind the house that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) did great honour to our country when he occupied that chair.
On the other hand, I was able to realize the difficulties encountered by the United Nations in the solution of the problems of underdeveloped countries suffering from hunger. While the problems have not all been solved, the results obtained so far are gigantic.
It must in fact be remembered that, in 1945, most African countries were either under colonial rule or under a protectorate or mandate not much different from colonial rule. The rush toward sovereignty in 1960 and 1961 is certainly epoch-making.
The movement of emancipation which is sweeping Asia and Africa cannot be reversed and, for the good of mankind we should give it our full support. Then, too, it is noteworthy that the emancipation which has taken place
External Affairs
in Africa has taken place peacefully, contrary to what was happening before the establishment of the United Nations.
There is a point I wish particularly to bring to my colleagues' attention. It has to do with the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization, known as the FAO. This organization was set up with the hope, expressed in the Atlantic charter, that a state of peace would be established which would ensure to all countries freedom from want. Today, chiefs of state, social workers, and economists are rightly concerned with the problems the world will have to face if no help is given to starving populations. This situation was described in the autumn of 1959 during a conversation on T.V. between the prime minister of England and the president of the United States. The prime minister of England was speaking about countries with underdeveloped economies, and Mr. Eisenhower, then president of the United States, had this to say:
In a way, I believe that the problem of the underdeveloped countries is more flexible and important for western civilization than that of the differences and quarrels between Soviet Russia and the western world. Today, 1,700 million human beings lack adequate food, shelter, and health services. Those people will not remain silent forever. They become aware of their fate and they compare it with ours. Unless we help them, they will eventually blow up. I think that the chief co-operative task facing the so-called civilized world, including the Soviets, and which the whole world should undertake together, is to see that the legitimate aspirations of those peoples are fulfilled. It is a problem in which everyone of us should take an interest, to see what he can do and how he can share in it.
And Mr. Macmillan went on:
I think, as you do, that it is not fair that we and our fellow citizens should enjoy all those things we have, houses, hospitals, education, etc. while those people are reduced to poverty and misery . ..
That is the most crucial problem that the world must face at this time. Already someone has described this situation as a real panic. In fact, while the rich nations, with a population of 400 million, whose annual income amounts to approximately $1,000 per person, and is as high as $2,000 in the United States, one billion people in Asia, Africa and Latin America, without mentioning communist China, must be satisfied with an annual income of $60, which hardly increases and is even growing less in some countries.
One has only to read the press reports and United Nations publications to realize the state of destitution existing in the world.

External Affairs
In the matter of food, it is recognized that the minimum number of calories needed by people in temperate countries is 2,700, but this figure may go as high as 4,500 according to the nature of the work performed. However, in underdeveloped countries, the ration is generally between 2,700 and 3,300 calories. In other words, 50 per cent of the the average consumption is 1,570 to 2,300 calories. In other words, 50 per cent of the population of the world is getting less than the bare minimum of calories to survive.
In the matter of health, world-wide disease control programs have been set up under the UN, with wonderful results. However, much remains to be done before adequate medical and hospital care is provided.
Whereas in the United States there is one doctor for every 800 people or so, and one hospital bed for every 101 people, and in Canada there is one doctor for every 950 people and one bed for every 77 people, in underdeveloped countries, there is only one doctor for 20,000, 40,000 and even 70,000 people, and one bed for 1,000, 2,000 and up to 3,000 people. If you add to that the fact that the ratio of illiterate people over 10 years of age varies from 40 to 90 per cent, you realize in what position mankind finds itself in facing the most fearsome economic problem, with its social, political and racial implications.
While the situation is of course serious, according to some humanists, what is worse is the indifference and perhaps also the ignorance of some people with respect to world politics. Canada carries its share of responsibility in that respect.
The immediate surpluses now owned by the "have" countries would only be a drop of water in an ocean of poverty, if we decided to give them away.
It must be recognized that commendable efforts have been made by the United States and Canada to find a means of meeting the basic needs of the "have not" countries.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) suggested, at a meeting of the NATO countries in 1957, that an international food bank be set up.
In early November 1959, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) made certain suggestions to the F.A.O. in Rome, but apparently met with little success.
Today, however, now that the government has decided to dispose of agricultural surpluses and restrict agricultural production, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agri-

culture seem less interested in pushing this food bank idea.
Canada would find itself in a ridiculous position today if we were called upon to supply products other than grain.
We did have pork surpluses. We were told a short time ago that we had 35 million pounds of surplus pork, but those reserves have been sold, and we no longer have a pork surplus. Perhaps we still have a surplus of butter and milk powder. With Canada's present agricultural policy, it can be said that we have practically no surpluses left to give away or distribute to starving countries.
And what will we be able to supply, a few months hence, in view of the defeatist policies now being followed by the present Minister of Agriculture in regard to price supports? We will be lucky if production can be maintained at a level adequate to meet our own needs and fill the orders from our remaining export markets.
It is true to say, and I quote from an editorial published in Terre de Chez Nous for May 6, 1959, that:
Every time agricultural surpluses reach a level substantially higher than the commercial marketing opportunities, we are given a great show. In the forefront are groups whose true intentions are camouflaged under high-sounding phrases. Government authorities quickly lose their heads and adopt measures that are often half-baked.
What an about-face since the statements made by the Prime Minister in 1957, when speaking in Saskatoon, as reported in the Western Producer for September 10, 1959.

Mr. Speaker, anyone with any sense of responsibility must recognize that expressing ideas on relations between countries in the world has become a delicate and even dangerous matter, because of the great international tensions which are constantly increasing. However, the position of a Canadian in this respect, is less risky, as Canada is in no way considered as a militarily aggressive country.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, we are proud to note the rate at which Canadian influence within the United Nations is increasing. The prestige of this country in that world organization is taking colossal proportions, considering that Canadian history is only four centuries old and that we scarcely have a population of 18 million. Relatively speaking, Canada compares favourably with many countries in the world.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, our strength is not based on physical or military power; it is rather a moral strength based on Christian and democratic values.
In the eyes of other nations, Canada will remain on the same level as the greatest world powers to the extent that she continues to set an example of complete respect for spiritual values while protecting human dignity to the fullest extent.
In external affairs the mission of Canada as of all other commonwealth countries and the other western- nations, is to maintain those Christian principles, as a vigorous and living reality in their practical application for they are the glory of our civilization and the best guarantee against a renewal of that gory experience we have known in the last two world wars, of millions of human beings destroying one another.
And speaking of Christian principles, on behalf of those Canadians I represent here, in

speechtext:
Of course, we realize that every individual has the natural and deeply human wish to see his life on earth last as long as possible. But, for the sake of future generations, would it not be more important if the ultimate goal of our life were the safeguarding, under every circumstance, of that invaluable treasure which we inherited from our two mother countries, i.e. a sound democracy with a Christian civilization, even if it cost us a few years of our lives?
I do not mean, Mr. Speaker, that we should strive to bring other powers to give up their ideologies so that we may substitute our own. That would be utopian. But our role

External Affairs
consists in providing peaceful community life while respecting the freedom all nations and individuals have of living according to their own convictions.
I cannot help endorsing here, and with pride, the only acceptable policy for a country like ours, a policy which has been most eloquently described by the representative of the people of Canada. Our newspapers have reported in laudatory terms the views of the people of Canada on the firm, clear and definite approach shown by the right hon. Prime Minister at the United Nations last September. A practical lesson in international policy, on the subject of colonialism, was served, with all the trimmings, to the Russian prime minister. For the glory of both France and the commonwealth, I should like to repeat here that part of the speech made by the Prime Minister of Canada:
Since the last war, seventeen colonies and dependent territories, totalling more than 40 million people, have been led by France to complete freedom. In the same period, fourteen colonies and dependent territories, totalling half a billion men, have achieved complete independence within the commonwealth. All told, it means that 600 million men, in more than 30 countries most of which are now represented in the United Nations, have achieved their freedom with the approval, encouragement and help of the United Kingdom, the commonwealth and France. Few countries can apeak here of colonialism with as much authority as we can, because our country was once a colony of France and of the United Kingdom. Our country was the first one which, about a century ago, achieved its development by constitutional means and managed to pass from colonial status to independence, without having to break family ties.
Descendants of France and of commonwealth countries, as well as all Canadians, are indeed grateful to the Prime Minister for having described so forcefully and clearly the humanitarian policy applied by our two mother countries throughout the years. Those words had to be said and repeated here in this house.
As a representative of French-speaking Canadians, this impels me to underline the significance for Canada of the African countries' admission to the United Nations. Everyone knows that, in most of those African countries (including several former French colonies) a good percentage of the population speaks French. That is why, in a recent speech, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) expressed the following ideas:
Canada is one of the only middle powers in the western world in a position to understand the problems of both the former British colonies and the former French colonies in Africa. This is why the efforts always exercised by French Canadians to
[Mr. Lafreniere.l
promote French thought throughout Canada take on a new importance that had been overlooked up to now.
This is where the active co-operation of the French Canadian becomes essential, not only for the Canadian cause, but especially for the cause of western civilization: that he may offer his services when a knowledge of French is necessary. Therefore, it is essential to the protection of our values that French Canadians take a positive stand in the assistance to be given to African countries. No one else is in a position to perform this duty which is, I say it again, altogether fundamental.
Mr. Speaker, this is an excellent opportunity for the government to consider increasing as much as possible the French representation at home and abroad, not only in the administration, but also in the government. It is a well known fact, Mr. Speaker, that the status of French speaking Canadians is not that of a minority in this country. They are partners on a fully equal basis.
According to international law, a minority has no real rights, but privileges. The right of having its own culture and language is acknowledged but, as a rule, its political rights are always limited. Such is not the case in Canada, because French is recognized as an official language. Since our country is of a bilingual and bi-cultural nature, other countries must be made aware of it, and this can only be done through the Department of External Affairs.
I know that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) is concerned about this problem, but he cannot instantly remedy the guilty negligence of the former administration on this point.
I now wish, Mr. Speaker, to express a few thoughts on the problem which seems most important to me and the most serious particularly at this time with regard to the relations between east and west, I mean assistance to underdeveloped countries.
Nowadays, Mr. Speaker, thanks to transport facilities, to the speed of information, the peoples of the world are closer to one another. Members of the great human family now live under the same roof, and we could even extend the analogy as far as to say that, when necessary, they eat at the same table. But as in this twentieth century we still have to deplore the fact that two thirds of the human beings on earth are living in hunger and poverty, here is the question that must be asked: How much longer will members of the same family tolerate that some live in wealth and luxury, having the best of foods to satisfy their appetite, when others are collapsing under the burden of misery and hunger?

That is why, Mr. Speaker, the executive director of the United Nations special funds, Mr. Paul Koffman, in the course of a recent session of the Economic and Social Council, made this impressive statement:
When the history of this twentieth century is written the outstanding event to be recorded will not be the first or second world war, nor the conquest of space, but the fact that one and three quarter billion human beings whose ancestors had accepted hunger, poverty and disease, decided to tolerate these no longer.
Such is, Mr. Speaker, the nature of the problem now threatening the world, and much of the responsibility falls on the western countries. Their task is to put forward, quickly and efficiently, a program of educational, technical and economic assistance.
I must say however in all fairness that the countries concerned, and in particular those which are members of NATO, are well aware of the seriousness and the urgency of the problem. With some colleagues, I had the opportunity, in June 1959, of representing Canada at the tenth anniversary Convention of NATO in London. My official function was that of economic rapporteur of subcommittee D-3 to which the 15 NATO members presented a brief on the common economic problems of the west.
I read those briefs and made a summary of them, from which you will allow me, sir, to quote a few lines, in order to indicate how well those nations understand the necessity of taking action. I quote:
Inaction might give rise to a peril much greater than the unpleasant prospect of being engulfed in a world where the ruling majority, impelled by envy and long pent-up resentment, might be in a position, by reason of its population and its vast territories, to exert on the west deadly economic if not military pressures. That danger is also that of a world where a triumphant communism would extend its roots in all directions. Furthermore, it would be foolhardy to underestimate the extent to which the communist system appeals to underdeveloped countries, although individual freedoms are sacrificed without mercy under it.
Such is, Mr. Speaker, the thought of the NATO countries, an organization of which Canada must remain an active member, the statements of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) to the contrary notwithstanding.
But, besides the economic aid program, we must lay emphasis on the educational program within those underdeveloped countries. Financial help and relief in the form of various products are only of a transistory nature. What counts is to give those people the necessary technical knowledge and training that
will enable them to take an active part in their development and to work themselves towards their industrial and commercial expansion.
Furthermore, any help extended to underdeveloped countries must not be considered by them or by us as outright charity inspired by sympathy and pity; that help, must be considered, as it is incidentally, as an invitation to an exchange of friendly services which eventually and effectively will be materially and morally profitable to both parties.
Indeed, besides performing that humanitarian deed absolutely necessary for the recovery of underdeveloped countries, the western countries, including Canada, will be opening up important future markets for the export of their products.
It is therefore a huge task and, in the light of a normal population increase throughout the world, we can expect that this world population will have increased twofold within forty years or so, but the stakes are worthwhile, since it means preventing war and safeguarding peace throughout the world by sheer efforts.
Before resuming my seat, Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the Secretary of State for External Affairs, his parliamentary secretary and his closest associates for the perseverance, tenacity and confidence they show on all occasions, as regards the possibility of disarmament.
I rejoiced recently when the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley) announced the award in my constituency of a $4 million contract for the production of 18 million cartridges for the Valcartier armoury. Thanks to that contract, 400 employees were able to keep their jobs which they might otherwise have lost. But, how happier would I be if I learned that those cartridges, instead of being used for war purposes were to be used for partridge shooting. Mr. Speaker, it would be too bad for the partridges! In any case, let us hope that those large amounts will one day be used to promote education and peace.
In any case, difficult though it may seem, disarmament still appears as a possibility.
One of the staunchest advocates of disarmament is probably our delegate to the United Nations, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who represents what Christian nations respect most, namely human dignity in all that the word implies. We can only wish him all the courage required under the circumstances, and express the hope that human intelligence, with the

External Affairs
aid of Providence, will succeed in creating systems favourable to peaceful coexistence of nations on this earth.

Mr. Speaker, seldom has this house engaged in a debate on external affairs at a time of greater world tension and anxiety than at this very moment. Some differences of opinion have been expressed in this debate already, particularly by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), with regard to certain aspects of the government's policy and with regard to certain policies being followed by some of the major powers in the world. I want to tell the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) that as he goes from nation to nation and as he speaks in the councils of the world our thoughts are with him, our best wishes are with him, and although we may disagree at times with particular policies, nevertheless with him we voice our opinions on the basis of what we believe to be in the best interests of our nation, in the best interests of freedom and in the best interests of peace in the world.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has earned for himself an excellent reputation in this country and in other parts of the world as a firm advocate of disarmament, and as a staunch supporter of a continuing ban on nuclear testing. We wish him well in all of these endeavours.
Spokesmen of the C.C.F.-New party group in the house have expressed full opposition to NATO, a position different from that taken by the Liberals. In recent months we have said that we have been disturbed that NATO has continued to be almost exclusively a military organization; that we feel more and more people are coming to the conclusion that Canada's best role in the preservation of peace and freedom is in more positive avenues than those offered by the NATO organization.
Over the years we in the C.C.F. movement, and our predecessors before us, have always been very firm and loyal supporters and admirers of the United Nations organization, and that faith remains. We wish to see everything possible done now and in the future to strengthen the United Nations organization and its machinery, since we feel that in this strengthening lies the best hope for peace in the world. We are admirers of the work, the contributions and efforts of the Secretary General of the United Nations, Mr. Dag Hammarskjold, and we view with alarm any and all efforts to downgrade his position, to divide his authority or to take other steps that would lessen the effective work of the United Nations. We are pleased that at this time the aftermath of the Cuban fiasco, to which so much thought is being given,
(Mr. Lafreniere.]
apparently has not prevented positive action, as far as we can tell, to bring peace to Laos, and we are pleased that Canada once again will be playing a constructive and positive role in this regard.
I listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lafreniere) with great interest and I certainly endorse what he said about the particular role that Canada can play because of the bilingual and bicultural nature of this country in assisting the development of the emergent French communities, particularly in Africa. I might say that for some considerable time I have been an advocate of Canada taking action similar to that announced by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) the other day. As far as I have been able to ascertain, and I am quite willing to be corrected, I was the first member of the house to spell out a program somewhat of the type that the government has followed. This was not an original idea with me. It was put forward in some of the French language newspapers of the country, but I felt it was an excellent idea worthy of endorsation and I was pleased to do so on March 4, 1960, in a speech delivered at Sir George Williams University, Montreal.
I took part in discussions of this question in the house following the proposal being made and when it was discussed as recently as July 14, 1960, the Secretary of State for External Affairs expressed interest but felt at that time that great difficulties presented themselves. I am pleased that some policy has been evolved and has been announced in the house. I am pleased that it has been given, as I was certain it would be, unanimous approval by members of all parties. I say to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that as the policy develops of assisting the French-speaking nations of Africa by suppling French-speaking teachers from this country and providing scholarships for training people from those countries at our universities, we shall be pleased to support at any time whatever further extension of this kind of program is practicable and will be of a helpful nature to these emergent nations.
The matter that I would imagine is on the minds of most hon. members more than any other is the recent unhappy experience in Cuba. I believe it is incumbent on members of the house to speak out frankly in this regard, to place their views on Hansard and make them known to the government. In due course the government will consider those views and I would hope that the expressions of opinion by members of the house may be helpful in the future in a constructive way.

Fidel Castro of Cuba came to power, I would think, with the best wishes of most people in the South American nations and with a great deal of good will on the part of many nations of the world in the hope that his government would improve economic standards of the people of Cuba. As a Canadian and a member of this house I was disturbed at a very early stage in his regime by the excesses in which I felt his administration was indulging. I was disturbed at the blood bath in that country in the early days of his regime. The first question I asked in the house after the opening of the session in 1959 was whether or not Canada had considered these atrocities and was prepared to send an appropriate note in this connection. I am not putting this forward to try to raise the issue as it was presented at that time. I merely put it forward to point out that the excesses of that administration have been abhorred by members of this group and we have felt that Canada should make its wishes known that this kind of thing should not be continued.
However, we have always taken the attitude that the type of government evolved in any given nation is really in the main the prerogative of the people of that nation and that there should be a minimum of outside influence and interference. We think that Fidel Castro and his regime came to power because of the abject poverty of the nation, because of exploitation and widespread disease, because of extensive illiteracy and the natural desire of the Cuban people for education, health, food and a rising standard of living.
We were opposed and we are opposed to action by the Soviet union, the United States or anyone else that would interfere with Cuba and the type of government that may be in office at any given time. We were opposed to the action that was taken by President Kennedy, as revealed in what has been written by well known and respected reporters, in promoting and assisting in almost every way the attack on Cuba by counterrevolutionary forces. We think that is a mistake in itself but we also think it is a mistake in its wider ramifications. We think that this kind of inappropriate action, far from being a deterrent to communism, merely plays into the hands of the communists, and that if President Kennedy should be determined to hand the nations of Latin America into the arms of the communists this is the way to go about it.
We suggest that Canada has an important role to play in speaking out at this time in this connection and saying in no uncertain terms to the United States administration what I and this group believe to be the
External Affairs
opinion of Canadians, namely, that this kind of risk, this kind of intervention, should not be proceeded with and is in fact a danger to the peace of the world.
Newsmen have been reporting on the aftermath of this intervention. One reporter, Frederick Nossal, says that the global scales are tipping against the United States. United States prestige in Japan is going down. Another reporter says that the Cuban affair worries the British; certainly, that is what we read in the British newspapers. Another headline in the Globe and Mail says, "Washington attitude alarms Great Britain".
The Globe and Mail, in an editorial on April 21, 1961, points out what, in their opinion, are the far-reaching results of this adventure. The editorial says, in part:
The results of this adventure seem likely to be far-reaching and unfortunate:
1.	The Castro regime, far from being overthrown, has been strengthened ...
2.	If Dr. Castro was not wholly in the communist camp before, these events may well put him there. Faced with an avowedly hostile United States, from which further attacks may come, he is likely to grasp all the more firmly the hand of friendship extended by the Soviet union.
3.	U.S. prestige has been badly damaged in Latin America .. .
4.	Most serious of all, the United States has damaged its moral position in the world as a peaceful, law-abiding nation, by seemingly resorting to undercover methods of warfare normally associated with the communist bloc.
This is an editorial from a respected Canadian newspaper, the Globe and Mail. Other reports have been forthcoming that are, I think, alarming and on which 1 think hon. members should speak out. I think it is our duty to speak out on this question. I certainly speak out, not in any sense of animosity to the United States, nor in any sense of being anti-American, but in the hope that if enough members of parliament speak out on this question statesmen in the United States might stop, look, listen and think about these representations coming from the parliament of Canada before they proceed with another adventure of this kind.
President Kennedy came to office with the almost unanimous goodwill of the people of the world. I have never known a statesman from a country outside our own who has had more widespread admiration here and in whom Canadians had more hope and faith than the present President of the United States. I am sorry to say that faith has been shaken and that goodwill that was his, accompanied as it was by much good will in other nations, has been withering away and falling off in the days since this misadventure. The past disturbs us, but the future prospects disturb us more.
I have in my hand a Globe and Mail article which quotes James Reston of the New York

External Affairs
Times service. The heading is "No Scapegoats". The subheading reads:
Kennedy shaken by Intelligence failure but takes full responsibility.
This sounds like a courageous thing to do, and I expect it is. However, I believe there are greater implications in this situation. The article says in part:
He took the decision to continue the training of the Cuban refugees with arms provided by the government, and for releasing the ships and gasoline to launch the attack at this time.
He did so against the advice of secretary of state Dean Rusk and under secretary of state Chester Bowles.
We read that one of the main reasons why President Kennedy has taken this attitude of full responsibility is that he does not wish to get into a partisan debate with the Republican party as to who was to blame for the original plans having gone wrong since they were formulated by the former administration. What disturbs me is the fact that this may be an indication that bi-partisan foreign policy in the United States, with the general agreement of the two major parties and their spokesmen, will once again lead to undertaking this kind of adventure, but having learned from this one will the next time undertake to overrun and overthrow the government of Cuba by using United States forces and by so doing will endanger the peace of the world. I think that would be a mistaken policy on the part of the United States government and I would hope that is not what is going to take place.
Mr. George Bain writes from Washington as follows:
The debate in the United States on Cuba policy has almost entirely ceased to entertain the question of whether that policy should be directed toward dislodging Premier Fidel Castro, and now concentrates only on how and when.
I hope there is a reconsideration in the councils of the United States. I would hope that there would be a change of policy. I hope that Canada will speak out in this regard.
The hon. member for Kootenay West raised this question on April 21, 1961 and at that time the Secretary of State for External Affairs, undoubtedly very worried and with his nerves taut, said something in reply that rather shocked me. He said:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether or not the hon. member wants us to declare war on the United States.
I hope that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in the tradition of this country, will make the strongest possible representations to the United States, in whatever way he believes best, to the effect that a misadventure of this kind should not be repeated. I believe, as I have said earlier,

that we all have a responsibility in this house. I think the official opposition has a very important responsibility. Yesterday the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) spoke but he did not contribute very much on this particular question not because, as I realize, he has not a very great knowledge in this field, but because he decided to say little about this subject. He said, as reported at page 4033 of Hansard for April 26, 1961:
At this time I am not going to press the minister beyond this. I am assuming that we have made our position known and that we are prepared to deal with the next step, which may or may not arise.
Then he said, in the same vein, that he hoped we, meaning Canada, would not hesitate to make our position known. I hope the Liberal party will make its position known in this house. The leader of the official opposition, I understand, is scheduled to speak in this debate. In view of the great experience he has had in the field of international affairs, the great reputation that has been his and the great achievements that have been his in helping to further the peace of the world, 1 would hope that he would address himself to this subject. I am certain that his words will be held in respect, not only in Canada but in the other nations of the world. I think that if enough of us speak out in strong terms to the United States as I hope the Canadian government has already done, we may well, along with other like-minded democrats in the world, so influence the United States that she will forgo any further adventures of this kind.
As I said earlier, this does not mean that we do not criticize-as we do-the excesses in Cuba. We value human life. When human life is exterminated, we should speak up. We value the processes of freedom and parliamentary democracy. We value our traditions. We sincerely feel that, for the peace and freedom of the world, when actions are taken which in our judgment are wrong, even though they be taken by our friends, we should make our own views abundantly clear. This we are doing.
I should now like to turn to a more positive statement of our external affairs position. We are continuing to spend very large sums of money for defence. Over the years we have taken the attitude that these defence expenditures or some of them could be better used if channelled in certain other ways. We feel that Canada's best role today is to have a strong conventional force available to the United Nations for use by the United Nations whenever our force is needed for United Nations police work. We view with great interest, as do all Canadians, the first cosmonaut and his achievements. I am an

optimist, along with the minister, as far as world affairs are concerned even though I have been pointing out some of the dangers. I think the competition between the Soviet union and the west is more likely in the years ahead to take place in the economic field, the scientific field, and in the field of conquering outer space. We are a small nation with a small population. We are wealthy in terms of our population but not in absolute terms. I should like the government to give some consideration to the question of whether or not we might be playing a small part-I know we are now playing a tiny part-shall we say, or a greater part in research, in association with other nations, particularly commonwealth nations, in the field of conquering outer space and delving into its scientific mysteries. I think this would be a more positive way in which to use some of the money that is now being spent on defence.
We have always been strong advocates of economic aid and economic assistance. Canada is doing a little bit but I am not too proud of the relatively small amount we are doing as compared with what we are doing in other fields. I have in my hand a statement given to me by the officials of the minister's department. It shows for economic aid an amount of under $60 million for the fiscal year 1959-60, just over $64 million for 1960-61, with estimates so far of roughly $62 million for 1961-62. There are other details-

Mr. Speaker, I am not trying to make the point that we are doing less now than we were doing a year ago or two years ago. I am merely pointing out these figures in order to show that, in relation to a present gross national product of over $30 billion, and expenditures on military establishments and defence expenditures of some $1.6 billion, this small expenditure is not good enough. I think we should do more. If the government could announce that this expenditure was being doubled or tripled or increased even more than that-for years we have said it should be 1 per cent of the gross national product and we have been given some support in recent days by a prominent spokesman for the Liberal party- or would move in this direction, I think it would be given the unanimous support of the members of this house and the general support of the Canadian nation.
I have made my own position clear. I have spoken on behalf of our group in the House
External Affairs
of Commons. I do this with a full realization that the Secretary of State for External Affairs is an old friend and an old colleague in this house over many years. Although he may have felt that I have been critical of his policy or the policy of other nations, I assure him that it has been done with the best of good will, with admiration for the person of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and in the fervent hope that, by working together and speaking out boldly, we may have some influence on the course of events in the world to the end that peace and freedom may be better secured.
