speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure indeed to take part in this debate, but I must confess that I had not expected to be taking part in it for perhaps another few moments. Therefore, if hon. members will just bear with me for about half a minute until I secure my brief notes, I shall proceed.
The first subject with which I should like to deal is that of the United Nations. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) in his remarks dealt with this particular subject at some considerable length. However, there are one or two additional items with which I should like to deal at this time. The first concerns world refugee year. The particular aspect of it of immediate interest to us was the movement to Canada of the third group of tubercular refugees that came here under this special program. As hon. members perhaps know, two groups of some 100 families came to Canada under this special program of world refugee year and just recently a third group have come to this country. Hon. members may recall that as one of our contributions to world refugee year, the government brought to this country two groups of tubercular refugees from refugee camps in Europe. The government paid transportation costs and maintenance costs for one year or until such time as the family became established. By January of this year only 51 refugees were still receiving treatment in sanitariums. So successful were those refugees in adjusting themselves to the Canadian environment and in becoming established in our communities that the government decided to extend the program and to admit a third group. In March of this year the third group composed of 272 persons, of whom 114 were tubercular, arrived in Canada. The total number of tubercular refugees, with their families, admitted to Canada in the three groups now stands at 826. The success of this program has been attributable in no small measure to the cooperation of the provincial governments

External Affairs
which have been responsible for the medical care and treatment of the refugees.
I feel sure that hon. members of this house and others in Canada will be very pleased with Canada's contribution to helping those people in the world who, through no fault of their own-other than that they disagreed, politically or economically, with the countries from which they came; for no other reason than that-because of the contraction of this unfortunate illness were left to a life of despair in refugee camps. We and certain other governments have done our best to provide homes and rehabilitation for them.
Another subject with which I should like to deal very briefly is the single convention on narcotic drugs. I think this is a subject of interest to quite a large number of hon. members. In this regard a conference to adopt a single convention on narcotic drugs was held at United Nations headquarters, New York, from January 21 until March 31 last.
More than 70 countries participated and our delegation played an important part in the negotiations which led to the adoption of a single convention on narcotic drugs. Canada signed the convention on March 31 last. To a very considerable extent the single convention is a consolidation of the existing multilateral treaties and protocols on narcotic drugs.
The convention, while recognizing the necessity of controlling existing sources of supplies, also takes into account the growing importance of synthetic narcotics brought about by continuing research in chemistry and pharmacology.
The adoption of the single convention will simplify and improve the procedures for the control of narcotic drugs and increase the effectiveness of the international organizations involved in combating the illicit drug trade.
It is, I think, heartening to reflect that the community of nations, despite their ideological differences, has been able to reach such substantial agreement in the field of narcotics control, where international co-operation is really very essential.
There are two items which have been referred to by various hon. members this afternoon, including the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Stinson) and the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger), I believe.
One is the subject of the so-called world food bank. As hon. members may recall, a resolution with regard to this matter was proposed by Canada last fall at the first part of the fifteenth general assembly of the United Nations. The subject was dealt with in the second committee, which deals with economic and social matters.

After a considerable amount of discussion and consultation with other delegations the resolution was brought forward and unanimously accepted in the second committee. This resolution requested, in essence, the food and agriculture organization, which was meeting in Home at the time, to investigate ways and means of providing emergency food supplies to countries which had suffered a disaster such as an earthquake, as happened in Chile a year ago, drought, or some other disaster. It would also assist countries where civil war or some other man-made unpleasantness had resulted.
This matter was referred to the food and agriculture organization for the purpose of working out a detailed plan which is to be submitted to the meeting of the economic and social council which is sitting in New York.
Incidentally, that particular body was properly constituted only last week, because there had been some difficulty in electing the eighteenth member. However, I should like to deal with this particular aspect of the economic and social problem a little later in my remarks.

The next item with which I should like to deal is the subject of the so-called experts

bank, which was also a Canadian initiative last fall. This subject was also referred to, of course, by the hon. member for York Centre.
For some time, under the project known as OPEX the United Nations, through its secretariat, has been able to secure the services of specialists in various governmental fields to assist countries under specific conditions. Until last fall one particular aspect of this problem had been rather neglected. I refer, again, to the question of an emergency and a situation such as occurred in Chile a year ago, an earthquake; civil war or other man-made or natural disaster. Because of these disasters public services in these countries might very often be very seriously disrupted. I refer to public services such as health, transportation, public administration and the like.
We felt that some effort should be made to provide specialists who could be called upon in an emergency and would not take six or eight months to recruit. To obtain properly qualified people to perform jobs in these fields may take some time. It requires some time to persuade people to leave good jobs in Canada and accept a perilous and uncertain job in some country far afield.
We felt that member countries of the United Nations should set up rosters of expert personnel from the civil service in the fields of public administration, transportation, health and the like, who could be called upon if a disaster occurred in some part of the world. These lists should be supplied to the secretariat. Then if a disaster occurred in country A, the government of country A could call on experts from Canada or whatever country they chose to come and assist in the emergency.
If this roster of experts were set up, it would not take weeks to provide experts. They could be provided through the United Nations, on request, almost instantly. This would greatly facilitate the rehabilitation of countries after a disaster had taken place.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the sad things about the United Nations, as far as reporting on it is concerned, is that one cannot tell all, so to speak, because a number of the many important negotiations taking place there are private or of a confidential nature. I would like, however, to make a few observations at this time regarding the
External Affairs
general characteristics of the fifteenth general assembly of the United Nations which just completed its work last Saturday.
As all hon. members will realize, the assembly started its work last September, and after a recess commencing shortly before Christmas and lasting until March 7, it resumed its work, which was completed, as I have mentioned, last Saturday.
The first half of the session saw the attendance of a great many world personalities. I do not think I need say more in this regard. In general terms the atmosphere during that portion of the session was very acrimonious. The cold war was in full swing and as a result it was very difficult for any country to accomplish very much.
During the second half of the session the atmosphere was quite different. There was a more conciliatory attitude and a number of things in fact were accomplished. During my remarks before six o'clock I mentioned the two initiatives that Canada launched during the fall session, and despite the acrimonious atmosphere the resolutions concerning the food bank and the experts bank were unanimously passed by the general assembly.
Last fall the Soviet union and associated countries launched a two-pronged attack in the United Nations. This was not new but was in fact a resumption of something that had been going on for a number of years. On this occasion there was more emphasis placed on it than before. The attack took two forms. It was, first, an attack on the secretary general both personally and upon his office. Second, the Soviet countries attempted to become the champions of the newly freed or liberated colonial peoples of Africa or of Asia. I am sure hon. members followed this subject in the newspapers and I do not wish to take up the time of the house by going into this subject in detail.
The attacks by the members of the Soviet group were very virulent indeed. The suggestion was made that the office of the secretary general should be replaced by a triumverate-three under secretaries. This obviously has the disadvantage of providing, in effect, a Soviet veto in regard to all the work of the secretariat. This proposition was based on the 1-1-1 formula, as it is sometimes called. It was proposed that one secretary general should be from the west, one from the Soviet group, and one from the neutral countries. Of course, any one of the three could exercise a veto in regard to the work done in the assembly. Since the secretariat is often charged with the responsibility of carrying out the resolutions passed by the general assembly, this would provide an effective veto over anything passed by the assembly.

External Affairs
There have been a number of explanations given in regard to this proposal. The most generally accepted one, heard in the United Nations and elsewhere, is that the United Nations has had the effect of blunting Soviet ambitions for ultimate world control. Since the United Nations has done this the Soviet union decided to try to either control the United Nations to suit its own purposes or render it ineffectual. There was some support at the outset for these two approaches made by the Soviet group but ultimately, I think it is quite safe to say, they both failed.
The attacks upon the secretary general were maintained in all the committees and persisted throughout. However, a little more than a week ago a resolution was before the general assembly concerning the Congo operation containing a paragraph referring to the work of the secretary general. The Soviet group requested a separate vote in respect of this particular paragraph with the intention of removing it from the resolution. I do not recall the exact vote, but from memory I would suggest that 83 countries voted in favour of retaining the paragraph and 11 voted against it, with the remaining number abstaining for one reason or another. The result of this vote was in effect a great vote of confidence in the secretary general personally, and I think we can take great encouragement from this. There was, of course, in general terms, this undercurrent throughout the last session of the general assembly, but the secretary general despite that undercurrent, and the almost unbelievable attacks both personally and against his office, not only survived but came out stronger than before.
There have been a great many changes in the United Nations within the last year. Those members who attended the United Nations session some years ago would notice now even greater changes. The first time I had the opportunity of attending at the United Nations was in 1955 and I can say that it is today quite a different organization from what it was then. In that year I had the pleasure of being a parliamentary observer working under the vice-chairman, the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), who was very helpful indeed at that time. I will always cherish with a great deal of pleasure my memory of that assistance.
Since that time the United Nations has expanded greatly. Indeed, 17 new countries became members last year. Membership in the United Nations now totals 99 member countries. Fourteen of these new countries are French-speaking African countries. I might say in this regard that because of Canada's cultural heritage a bond of friendship was established with these countries. We did our best to develop that friendship

and I feel safe in saying that we now have very close and friendly relationships with those African members.
I would particularly like to mention those individuals who contributed in this regard. One is a member of our delegation, the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Asselin), who did a great deal of outstanding work in developing close relationships between this country and the new French-African countries. Indeed, one or two other members were very helpful in this regard. These numbers were parliamentary observers. One is the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Parizeau), and the other is the hon. member for St. Ann (Mr. Loiselle), who did a great deal of work in helping us in this regard.
As the Secretary of State for External Affairs pointed out earlier in a previous announcement-and I think it is perhaps worth while mentioning in this context-the Canadian government has decided on a program of assisting in the education of students from those French-African territories to the amount of $300,000 a year. This has been much appreciated in those areas and is probably the best kind of work which we can do at the present time to help the people in those countries.
Another different aspect of the United Nations this year is the changing of the so-called blocs in the United Nations. We often hear people speak of the Latin American bloc, the Asian-African bloc, and so on. Some of those blocs have shown considerable evidence that they are changing in character or are dividing into groups. Because of the large number of new African countries, there is a tendency to find an African group rather than an Asian-African group. This is an interesting trend to those who are familiar with the United Nations, and I think it is perhaps worthy of note.
Another very important thing, of course, is the change in the voting strength in the United Nations. A few years ago the western European group, the Latin American group and some of the commonwealth countries made up the majority of the voting strength in the United Nations. Now, with the Asian and African countries, 45 out of the 99 votes belong to the Asian and African countries. This has greatly affected the tactical situation in the United Nations from everybody's point of view. Again, it is something that has happened in the last assembly which has changed the whole picture of the United Nations.
These may be self-evident things, but I think it is worth while reminding people of them because they are factors in this whole changing, and very rapidly changing, picture of the United Nations. At one time it was

said that if the Asian-African countries and the Soviet group all got together they would have what is known as "blocking third" in the plenary meetings of the assembly, where a two thirds votes is necessary. But this whole situation has changed because the countries of Africa and Asia have themselves almost half of the votes of the assembly. This has a great effect on the way resolutions are worded and the way they are presented in order to meet these fundamental changes in the character and make-up of the United Nations. These changes have altered Canada's own role at the United Nations.
In the late 1940's and middle 1950's it was often said that Canada formed a sort of link between the Soviet group countries and the western countries. Judging from my own experience in the United Nations, Mr. Speaker, I would say that we still do that from time to time but perhaps one of the new roles that Canada has in this context is that we now tend to form, as well, a link between some of the western countries and the countries in Asia and Africa. We also act as a stabilizing influence with our own groups. In this regard I also think of countries such as Norway with which Canada often works at the United Nations, and other smaller countries such as New Zealand and Ireland. I could mention many others. In addition to the link that I mentioned previously, I think the role of these countries is also that of extending or acting as a link between the Asian and African countries and the countries of western Europe and North America. I think this is a very important thing. Again, it is a fairly self-evident matter, but I think it is worth bringing to your attention, sir. Perhaps it is only a shift in emphasis but it is indeed a shift.
Another thing that is worth mentioning is the general preoccupation of countries, particularly in Africa, with the desire to catch up, particularly economically, with the other countries of the world. It is my impression that those countries are not especially interested in particular economic and political theories. It seems to me this attitude is one in which the position is taken that while economic and political theories are very fine for those who have the luxury to afford them, these countries have to adjust to the particular economic and political systems that they have to suit their own stage of development, and they are more interested in catching up economically and providing the necessities of life for their people than they are in the other matters.
Sometimes a number of those newer countries in various parts of the world have perhaps behaved in a manner which some
External Affairs
of us might consider to be irresponsible according to our standards. Although the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) seemed to feel rather depressed about the outlook in the United Nations, my own feeling is that while some of these newer countries in a new situation are expressing themselves perhaps for the first time in the world organization, and while some of their activities might seem less than desirable, I think in two or three years, this matter will certainly adjust itself. I do not think there are any grounds for pessimism in that regard whatsoever.
One interesting observation is the fact that many of the new African states have totally different views. They do not all think alike. A good example, of course, is the Congo operation and the approach to what should be done in that particular area. Most of the African countries have quite different methods of approach to this problem. There is one thing they all have in common, and that is the common desire to have the cold war kept out of Africa, and the African countries left alone to develop the continent themselves. As a matter of fact, I think most hon. members will agree that that will be very commendable indeed.
This last observation also brings up another trend which might be of interest. There is evidence of a possible trend developing in the United Nations away from the original idea of universality. I refer to the new trend of regional emphasis. By that I mean that one heard constantly in speeches on the Congo that the Congo situation was an African problem and should be left largely to the Africans themselves. Dr. Nkrumah, the president of Ghana, in his last speech in the assembly and in his remarks to the advisory committee, suggested that this was an African problem and should be left to the Africans to solve. The recent Cuban crisis was another example. It was emphasized that the situation in Cuba was a matter for the organization of American states to look after. Whether these trends are going to develop and continue to develop I do not know, but they are worthy of notice, because it is a slightly different concept of the United Nations, slightly different from that one formerly had of that body, because the trend is toward having certain areas or regions of the world look after their own problems. This may be an inevitable development, I do not know. It remains to be seen. Again I mention this because it is something that has perhaps appeared at this particular session to a greater degree than before.
As the hon. member for Essex East pointed out, there are a number of problems at the

External Affairs
United Nations, and one of them is the question of financing. This has been a very serious problem indeed at this session. One of the big problems at the United Nations for the past two or three years has been how to finance these various peace-keeping operations, first of all UNEF in the Middle East or Near East, whichever way you wish to classify it, and then, of course, the Congo operation. The countries in the Soviet group will not contribute anything toward these peace-keeping operations and, unfortunately, there are also some other countries which behave in the same way for reasons best known to themselves. Some of these countries claim they cannot afford to pay, which may well be the case, of course, and we can understand this particularly in the case of the newly developing countries.
However, the fact that these operations have been authorized by the general assembly presents a very interesting problem. On the one hand, you have the general assembly passing resolutions demanding that certain things be done in the Near East or, most recently, of course, in the Congo. On the other hand, you have, as we witnessed last Saturday night, a situation where the assembly will not vote the money to carry out the instructions it has passed. It is a very odd sort of position and, as I have already mentioned, the reason is the fact that a number of countries feel that for these peace-keeping operations the regular scale of assessments should not be carried out but rather some new scale of assessment should be devised.
There were long discussions and many negotiations over this matter during the last session of the assembly, and eventually a resolution was put forward by Pakistan, Ghana and others temporarily to tide over the United Nations financially until next fall. In conjunction with this, of course, Canada promoted a resolution which would appoint a group of countries to examine thoroughly the question of assessments as far as specialized peacekeeping operations are concerned.
I do not wish to take up the time of the house by going into the details of this matter. I should like to say that after a great deal of difficulty Saturday evening and after several votes the resolution sponsored by Pakistan, Ghana and others was finally passed which permitted the United Nations to carry on its Congo activities until the fall. I might say that I do not think it was generally realized how close this operation came to failing completely. On the first vote on this subject, which was taken around eleven o'clock last Saturday evening, the financing resolution was defeated. This would have meant that the secretary general would have had no funds whatsoever to carry on the Congo operation

and, indeed, there was some question whether the United Nations itself could have carried on because of the various borrowing operations that had gone on.
For some reason or other this did not seem to be appreciated by a number of member states and it took a very considerable amount of work on the part of the Canadian delegation and other associated delegations to change enough people's minds so that by about five or six o'clock in the morning the interim financing resolution was passed. After that the Canadian resolution successfully passed as well. It is a very real problem. I agree with the hon. member for Essex East when he says it is a very serious problem and some arrangement is going to have to be made at the next session of the general assembly. Otherwise I do not know what the result will ultimately be.
The hon. member for Essex East mentioned another subject having to do with the expansion of the security council and the expansion of the economic and social council. He pointed out, as I recall, that since the United Nations had grown so greatly in membership these councils should be expanded and that this would be a worthy field of endeavour in which to have Canada take part. I quite agree with the hon. member. Indeed, this was one of Canada's projects at the United Nations last fall. Unfortunately it was not very successful because the Soviet union blocked any enlargement of either of these councils and insisted that the question of China should be settled before any charter revision should take place. As a result, a number of the newer countries in Asia and Africa which feel they are not represented have put great pressure on countries in western Europe and, indeed, in the commonwealth, eastern Europe and Latin America as well, to give up one or more of the seats they hold on the security council or the economic and social council in favour of some of the newer nations of the world. It is a sort of share the wealth proposition.
This is highly unsatisfactory because all it does is perpetuate injustice. If some of the newer groupings in the United Nations are able to force some of the other groups to give up some of their seats, this may temporarily effect some sort of arrangement but it is not a very satisfactory solution. The only real solution to the problem is the expansion of both councils and this, of course, cannot be done until the Soviet union permits it under present arrangements in the United Nations.
Another thing in this regard that has happened as a result of this situation is that until the very end of the last assembly the

economic and social council was not constituted because India and Belgium were the two candidates for seats and neither one would agree to withdraw. They each had 45 votes and a two thirds vote was impossible under the circumstances. This happened a year ago in the security council elections as between Turkey and Poland, and hon. members may recall that Canada took a rather active part in settling that difficulty. But some permanent arrangement must be made with respect to these councils so that every year at the United Nations we do not have the same acrimonious argument as to what country is going to fill what position on which council, and I would agree with the hon. member for Essex East that that is something that should be worked out. However, unfortunately it is not in our hands.
I see that my time is up, Mr. Speaker, and I was wondering whether I might, by leave of the house, continue for five or ten minutes as there is another matter with which I should like to deal.
