speechtext:
I thank hon. members and I appreciate very much their courtesy. The last matter I should like to deal with concerns the remarks of the hon. member for Essex East with respect to the United Nations police force, and I wish to refer to page 4034 of Hansard for yesterday where the hon. member for Essex East is recorded as having said:
We might as well admit that the experience in the Congo portrays a weakness in the United Nations police force as it is at present constituted when the nations retain authority over their troops.
I think the distinguished hon. member for Essex East perhaps had something else in mind when he made that statement. As the hon. member well knows, when countries turn over troops to the United Nations command they do not have effective operating control over those troops. It is true they do have control to the extent that if country A contributes so many troops to the United Nations command it can, on request to the secretary general, withdraw those troops. I am sure that is probably what the hon. member for Essex East intended, but I think his remarks perhaps did create the impression that if country A supplied troops to the United Nations command, country A exercised actual control over the use of the troops while under this command, and I thought the hon. member would not object if I clarified the situation.
A little farther down on page 4034 the hon. member for Essex East suggested that
External Affairs
one of the most effective things Canada could do, in addition to putting forward a substantive proposal in the field of disarmament, would be to put forward, after careful preparatory work, a scheme for an effective United Nations force which must take its place in a disarmed world if that should ever eventuate. The hon. member quoted, in support of his position, a statement by the secretary of state, Dean Rusk, when he said:
-the experience in the Congo suggests that we must turn once more to the possibility of constituting a permanent United Nations force specifically trained and equipped and held in readiness for immediate use.
In connection with the argument for having a permanent force to meet a situation of the type in the Congo, it might be of interest to note the following comments of the secretary general, Mr. Dag Hammarskjold, as found on pages 3 and 4 of the introduction to the annual report of the secretary general on the work of the organization, general assembly official records, fifteenth session, supplement No. 1A (A/4390/Add.l):
I have mentioned the need for some strengthening of the secretariat on the military side. This, in the light of recent experience, would be my reply, as regards actions by the United Nations, to those who have found in the Congo developments new reasons for the organization of a standing United Nations force. As I have already clarified my views on this problem in earlier reports to the general assembly, I have no reason to go into the matter in any detail here. It should, however, be stressed that the Congo experience has strengthened my conviction that the organization of a standing United Nations force would represent an unnecessary and impractical measure, especially in view of the fact that every new situation and crisis which the organization will have to face is likely to present new problems as to the best adjustment of the composition of a force, its equipment, its training and its organization.
It is an entirely different matter if governments, in a position and willing to do so, would maintain a state of preparedness so as to be able to meet possible demands from the United Nations. And it is also an entirely different matter, for the organization itself, to have a state of preparedness with considerable flexibility and in the hands of a qualified staff which quickly and smoothly can adjust their plans to new situations and assist the secretary general in the crucially important first stages of the execution of a decision by the main organs to set up a United Nations force, whatever its type or task.
In these circumstances, a Canadian initiative at this time along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Essex East might not be very productive of good results. This is not to say that a proposal to this effect should not be made at some appropriate time in the future. In this connection, we have in mind that the question of the United Nations peacekeeping machinery might be one of the subjects which an ad hoc committee of the disarmament commission could carefully pursue.

External Affairs
I should like to point out that one of the suggestions we have made in respect of disarmament, which I know is procedural as the hon. member for Essex East has pointed out but is still rather important, is that when the negotiating body on disarmament which will be set up outside of the United Nations later this summer is constituted, there must be some liaison between this body and the United Nations. We feel that the United Nations disarmament commission, which is composed of 99 member states, would be the appropriate body for liaison on the subject of disarmament between the negotiating body, whatever its size and composition may be, and the United Nations. We feel that a negotiating body composed of 12, 13 or 14-whatever the number of nations that may comprise this body-should report periodically to the United Nations through the disarmament commission. We feel also, in turn, that member states of the United Nations who have ideas and suggestions on disarmament should be able to transmit those ideas and suggestions for consideration by the negotiating body through the disarmament commission.
We feel also that the disarmament commission could very well set up ad hoc committees to study specific aspects of the problem of disarmament. One of the things we feel the disarmament commission should set up an ad hoc committee to discuss and carefully look into is this question of peace-keeping machinery when disarmament is largely achieved. It is a most important matter and many member states of the United Nations could very effectively serve on such a committee. When I say an ad hoc committee, I mean a committee composed of perhaps 10, 15 or 20 states. Perhaps the non-nuclear powers could very well work out an effective scheme for peace-keeping machinery. It is something that will take a long time to do.
Some people might say, why set up a committee? Why not have the whole disarmament commission study the problem? Those who have worked on committees and commissions know that 99 countries do not form a very effective committee for the conduct of business. Perhaps a subcommittee of 15 or 20 countries would do this job very much better. I mention this in passing. This whole problem of working out peace-keeping machinery will need long and continued effort. It is something that will take a great deal of thought and study, something which the committee on disarmament might very well do.
In conclusion, there is one other matter I should like to mention. Again, it relates to this question of peace-keeping machinery. As reported on page 4036 of yesterday's Hansard, the hon. member for Essex East inquired about what type of international police force

should be established to preserve international peace and security. He asked what principles of international law should perhaps govern such forces. I can assure the hon. member that we have been giving very close attention to this problem. It is one of the most important problems to be solved if we are to be able to reach the final stages of general disarmament.
As the hon. member is doubtless aware, there have been a number of books and pamphlets issued proposing plans for international peace-keeping forces. Ideas in connection with this part of the general disarmament plans put forward by the west at Geneva last year were discussed between the delegates of the western five nations at the 10-nation disarmament conference. I would say, Mr. Speaker, that the difficult part of the problem is not how to make a plan for creating a force. Competent military staff officers could do this very quickly. The subject, especially as it relates to United Nations peace-keeping forces under present world conditions, has been under study by officers of the Department of National Defence as well as by officers of external affairs, and certain general conclusions have been reached. Officers of the Canadian defence services are well able to carry out a useful and practical study of this kind in view of Canada's experience in the several peace-keeping efforts of the United Nations.
The real problem, Mr. Speaker, is not how to organize, administer and operate such a force from the purely military viewpoint. The question is how it is to be controlled politically. We all know that at the present time these forces are under the control of the secretary general, and at the moment the secretary general is not accepted by the Soviet union. The five members of the security council who have the veto certainly do not agree on any of the major political problems in the world. As the remarks of the hon. member for Essex East indicate, the difficulty in this connection arises from the fact that the political objects of the communist countries led by the Soviet union and those of the countries of the west are, in most cases, opposed, I think we should all agree with that.
I should like to read an extract from a statement made by Mr. Zorin, deputy foreign minister of the Soviet union, during the discussion of the question of international armed forces in Geneva upon the resumption of talks in June, 1960. It reads:
The western powers submitted a proposal to create a so-called international armed force. But what would this lead to? It would lead to the world continuing to live as before, in fear of the use of weapons. Instead of national armies there would be created an international army, which would in fact be the army of one side directed against the other side. We must look at things

realistically. The world today consists of two parts -one socialist and the other capitalist.
This was before they divided the world into three parts.
It is clear to everyone that neither side will agree to the other side dominating the international armed force. It is absolutely clear that the western powers would not agree to the socialist countries playing a leading role in such a force. And we would not agree to assign such a role to the western powers.
Thus, it would be wrong and unrealistic to set out to create an international armed force. It would be another matter if we agree to place at the disposal of the security council, when necessary, in order to ensure the maintenance of peace, units from the contingents of police (militia) remaining at the disposal of states after the implementation of general and complete disarmament.
That is an entirely realistic measure which is also in accordance with the provisions of the United Nations charter, and it is provided for in our new proposals-
-"our new proposals" being, of course, the Soviet union proposals of the day.
Also in the statement which introduced the Soviet disarmament plan of June 2, 1960, the following sentence occurred:
Of course, such police (militia) detachments may be used solely for the purpose of maintaining peace among nations, not for the suppression of peoples who are struggling for their independence and social progress, and not for interference in the internal affairs of states.
From this hon. members will see that the Soviet union does not intend that there should be any peace-keeping force set up over whose operations it will not have a veto. This is confirmed by their attacks on the way in which the secretary general has interpreted and carried out the provisions of the security council resolutions dealing with the Congo. The Soviet union according to its own statements and actions is insisting that no peace-keeping force shall be used in a manner which is inconsistent with its own objects in promoting what it calls the "struggle for independence and social progress". Of course for the western nations and I think for the majority of other members of the United Nations any peace-keeping force, if it is to be worthy of the name, must not be subject to the veto of any nation or minority group of nations. How to devise an organization or modify the existing organization of the United Nations so to be able to carry out the function of political control and direction of the United Nations peace-keeping force is as yet an unsolved problem. It is our intention to continue to try to find a solution, in consultation with other like-minded nations, and especially with those with whom we are associated in disarmament negotiations.
There are a number of other things with which I should like to deal but I do not propose to request further time of the house.
External Affairs
I greatly appreciate the extra time that has been given to me. On another occasion I will deal with the other matters I have in mind.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity of taking part in this debate- perhaps I should not call it a debate but rather a discussion on foreign affairs-even though there is not that noisy, controversial and tense atmosphere we find in the house if we are talking for instance, about the unemployment insurance fund or even the support price for soya beans. But even though one might not gather it from the calm atmosphere of the house, Mr. Speaker, we are dealing with fundamental matters which affect the very survival of our nation and of humanity.
Before I proceed further, if I may, I should like to associate myself with what the minister said yesterday in appreciation of the intelligent, selfless and devoted service of the members of his department from the deputy minister down. He will know that I do this in no formal sense because perhaps no one in this house has more cause than I have to be grateful for the work of that department. I hope it will not make the minister feel uncomfortable if I tell him also that we on this side of the house also appreciate the sincere and honourable efforts he is making on behalf of all Canadians, as the spokesman of the government and indeed of Canada, to contribute to those causes, policies and developments which are making, we hope, for peace in a dangerous world. In this tribute to the minister I should like to include the parliamentary secretary who has just spoken to us and who has worked so hard and so long at the United Nations assembly.
Perhaps that should be the end of my complimentary references but, Mr. Speaker, I should like to add this observation. It is sometimes said by my hon. friends on my extreme right geographically that there is no difference between the two old parties that have together made, I think, a worthy contribution to the building of our nation. May I say that there is every difference in domestic affairs and that we show those differences in the House of Commons. However, there is no difference between us in our joint desire to support, on behalf of the Canadian people, policies that will bring peace and security to our country and to the world. We are at one in those objectives even though we may, do and will differ at times on how we should reach them.
We are at one in our support for the new commonwealth and for the United Nations.

External Affairs
must be known by anyone who has been following the development of the North Atlantic treaty organization in the last year.
When we mention these things it is only with the hope that these trends can be changed. The chancellor of the west German republic, who is one of the strongest and most fervent supporters of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, had this to say in Texas the other day:
It looked for a time as if NATO were going to fall apart.
I should add that he went on to say that as a result of his visit to Washington he felt a little better about it.
The minister will know that the recent secretary general of NATO, Mr. Spaak, who has worked so hard and brilliantly for the organization, has had some frank and worried things to say about its future. Perhaps at this point I should pay my respects to the new secretary general who I think will undoubtedly serve the organization in the same way as did his predecessors, Mr. Spaak and Lord Ismay. I refer, of course, to Mr. Stikker who was once a distinguished foreign minister of his country, the Netherlands.
The reasons for our worry on this side- I am sure the minister, though he may be inhibited in saying these things publicly, at times shares these worries-are obvious. We feel on this side that NATO has not adapted its defence strategy to new circumstances, new threats, new situations, confronting it in the last few years. One fear for the future, surely, is in an over-reliance on nuclear weapons. To rely on nuclear retaliation alone, or for a nation to risk its existence by deliberately depending on a strategy which permits of no alternative but annihilation or capitulation in the face of every threat, is certainly a very dangerous situation. That is something that we want to avoid in NATO. To avoid it we have to strengthen NATO's conventional forces so that the organization will not have to rely too much even on tactical nuclear retaliation.
Another danger facing the organization is the introduction of colonial problems and difficulties into NATO in areas which are technically outside the NATO zone but which in fact cannot help but have an effect on NATO itself. These colonial difficulties have, I am sure, caused division and disturbance, and perhaps at times, some distress inside NATO. It will be difficult I would think, to have the kind of co-operation which is required in the North Atlantic treaty organization, if there is division between the members of NATO in respect of matters outside- divisions which reflect themselves also in

policies at the United Nations. It may even be dangerous for the future, if we have to keep trying to relate co-operation in Paris to conflict at New York.
There is another worry developing in NATO. At least one member does not seem to share the views of practically all the others, that the direction must be toward greater collaboration and integration, both political and in defence.
As one who believes in this organization, I hope that these difficulties will be surmounted; that these dangers will be overcome so that NATO will be stronger both in the field of collective defence, and collective nonmilitary action because, after all, strength is more than military.
I now want to say a few words about the United Nations. We have heard, with interest, a great deal about the United Nations from the parliamentary secretary this afternoon and this evening, and from the minister yesterday. As with NATO, I do not think it is being unduly pessimistic to say that the United Nations is facing very difficult times at present. I could not help being impressed by an article in Foreign Affairs for April, 1961 by Mr. Hamilton Fish Armstrong, one of the great supporters of the United Nations over the years, one who was also present at the founding conference at San Francisco in 1945. Under the title "U.N. on Trial", he had this to say:
In the closing days of the general assembly last December one heard even responsible heads of delegations remark, sadly, bitterly: "The United Nations is done for."
He goes on to say:
The United Nations, though not yet done for, is indeed on trial for its life-
Perhaps that is a little over-dramatic but there is no doubt, as some hon. members pointed out yesterday, that we are facing new problems, new difficulties, and at least some new dangers at the United Nations. We are doing this at a time when it is more essential to preserve and strengthen this world organization than perhaps at any time in its history. I say that because, as the international situation deteriorates, that is the time when the United Nations should be most effective. It should also be more effective now than it was ten years ago because it is a better reflection of the world in which we live.
It is a more complicated, at times, a more disturbing reflection; 99 members, 45 of whom as the parliamentary secretary pointed out a few moments ago, come from Asia and Africa. But with all its complexities, the difficulties and the irritations; with the large new membership and with the shifting

of influence and authority to new nations, recently colonial, suspicious, sensitive, with all of that, I venture to say that this organization now reflects the world in which we live probably more accurately than that which we set up in San Francisco, which carried on the traditions, the diplomatic procedures, the political courtesies and conventions of western Europe of the nineteenth century and the league of nations in the 1930's.
We could all perhaps adjust ourselves to those changes without difficulty if we were allowed to do so by the communist bloc inside the United Nations. Yet last autumn Mr. Khrushchev showed that he was even willing to take the risk of destroying the world organization if it got in his way and he could not alter it. He showed this in the attitude of his government toward United Nations intervention in the Congo and in Africa generally.
He has also shown it in his attack on the Secretary General of the United Nations. I congratulate the minister, the parliamentary secretary and, indeed, the government on the way in which they have stood up for this great man. One of the hopeful developments in the last two or three months, after some very worrying times last fall, is the way in which the secretary general has managed to rally support around him. His position is stronger today than it was a few months ago. But the communist bloc has made it clear, I think beyond doubt, that they will do their best from now on to destroy not only this man because he has got in their way, as Trygve Lie got in their way, but also the office of secretary general. That is what in fact their proposal would amount to. As the parliamentary secretary pointed out, their proposal called for three secretaries general. Putting the office into commission with a communist, a non-communist and an anti-communist, simply means frustrating and hamstringing it so that it could not work at all. Indeed, the alternative proposal put forward, I think by India, for assisting the secretary general with three deputy secretaries general, one communist, one non-communist and one anti-communist and which, superficially, seems to be a more reasonable and perhaps workable proposal, might very well have the same ultimate effect itself on the office.
If the United Nations is to survive and remain strong it will be because the middle powers, both the uncommitted and the committed middle powers rally around an organization which is the one organization that can save them as a force in the nuclear world. In return, they are the ones, these middle powers, that can save the organization.
External Affairs
The minister had a good deal to say about disarmament. It is very hard at times-perhaps not so hard for the minister who is not a cynical person-not to become cynical about the absence of progress made in this vitally important field.
I have been concerned with disarmament conferences and commissions and developments since the first league of nations disarmament conference in 1932. At that time I think we got about as far after the first month of that meeting as we have got now. This is no argument for slowing down our efforts, of course, but it is an indication of the complexities and difficulties of the problem. Yet, I cannot refrain from pointing out, there are many decisions to be made by the Canadian government, especially in the field of defence, which are dependent upon progress being made in disarmament, so we are told. There is also the resolution supported by the Canadian delegation last autumn, the Irish resolution, I think, to prevent the extension of nuclear weapons to countries not now possessing them. This was supported by the Canadian delegation and I am certainly glad that support was given, but it depended we are told, on significant progress in the immediate future in the disarmament negotiations. I would hope that if there is not the kind of significant progress which the minister may have had in mind when that resolution was put forward, that this will not be used as a reason for abandoning the resolution.
Yesterday the minister mentioned the question of nuclear tests. I do not know how long-at least two or three years now-we have been struggling with that specific and concrete problem. Our hopes go up and down. There was a time when it looked as if the powers were almost on the verge of an agreement. Now they are further away from an agreement than they were six months ago.
Yesterday the minister explained why an agreement had not yet been achieved. With the Russian position at Geneva now falling back on the veto over control arrangements, I do not know how it is going to be achieved. However, the minister did say that notwithstanding, during the period of these discussions no nuclear tests had taken place. I wonder how we know that? If we can be sure that during those three years no nuclear tests took place, if we can be sure of that, then we do not need to worry about control arrangements in a nuclear test agreement. I hope no nuclear tests have taken place, but the fact that we have to insist, and rightly so, on control and inspection arrangements indicates that presumably we do not know whether or not they have.

External Affairs
I now come back to our own continent, and I should like to say a few words about our relations with the United States, especially in connection with the current Cuban problem, something that has been touched on by nearly everyone who has spoken in this debate. The minister said yesterday in connection with this delicate and dangerous situation, and of course he was right, that this is a time for cool-headed action and words. I think that is true. He might pass that on to his colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees).
Mr. Speaker, we will not be able to understand-at least I am not able to understand- the immediate significance of the Cuban situation without studying it against the background of general Latin American developments over recent years. Social and economic revolution is taking place in certain Latin American countries. I think that is both inevitable and desirable. Mr. Macmillan's winds of change are blowing in Latin America, and not only in Cuba where they have achieved destructive gale force.
This is happening in many Latin American countries. It is one of the reasons why I am glad we have extended our representation in that part of the world. Many of those who are interested in this social and economic evolutionary development in those Latin American countries are greatly attracted, or at least were greatly attracted, by what has happened in Cuba. Many of these people abhor communism just as they also abhor some of the dictatorial non-communist rulers that they have been subjected to in their own countries. The difference between the two tyrannies, however, is that a local tyranny is only local but a communist tyranny is an international one. That is a big difference. And behind all these social and economic movements in Latin America, or in any country of the world, lurk the forces of communist imperialism, who are hiding in the background, perhaps not responsible for the initial surges and developments but ready there to exploit them and to take charge of them.
As I see it, Mr. Speaker, intervention from outside against economic and social change is both futile and dangerous. If it were only a question of a local dictator perhaps there would not be the problem in all its dangerous implications that we find in Cuba today. But that problem becomes infinitely more dangerous, more difficult and more complicated when the dictator has behind him those international forces that I have been talking about, the international communist conspiracy. That has been the situation in Cuba, of course. Something that started out as a social and economic revolution, which won the support of practically everybody interested in human

progress, the support of practically everybody in the United States and in most of the Latin American countries except the dictatorial ones, has been taken over by international communist forces.
I think that what happened last week in regard to the policy of intervention by the United States was a mistake. Having in mind the way the landings worked out, it was certainly not very successful. Yet we would be wise not to lose our sense of proportion in regard to this matter. We would certainly be most foolish if our reaction were to assimilate United States policy with Soviet policy in Budapest, the Congo, or any other part of the world. The United States is our neighbour and friend. It is a free democracy where public opinion can express itself, where mistakes are made known and can be corrected. That does not apply in communist dictatorships. Furthermore, the United States today is the only power strong enough to provide the nuclear deterrent which, until there is general disarmament and we can find a stronger foundation for peace than force, is absolutely essential for the preservation even of the kind of peace which we have. Because of its strength the United States alone today can give us leadership as we face powerful and aggressive empires whom we have good cause to fear. Therefore, surely it is in our interests as Canadians to try whenever we can to support the United States to the very limit of our ability as a member of the coalition of which we are a member but to support her in the way which is both best for the coalition and best for ourselves.
We should rejoice when United States leadership is strong and wise and we should lament when things go wrong. But lamenting in that way is very different from getting almost a kind of sly satisfaction out of some American default or some American mistake; a kind of satisfaction based in part on envy. When mistakes are made, and I think a mistake was made by the United States government in this Cuban matter, that is the time to try to help to put things right rather than indulge in purely negative criticism.
Certainly Cuba presents one of these situations. We should not forget that the intervention which took place was not by Batista Cubans but, so far as I know, for the most part by Cubans who had fought against Batista in the early days of the revolution. That does not alter the fact that the intervention was a failure almost to the point of a fiasco, and the United States cannot escape some responsibility for both the intervention and for the failure.
I know that up to that time the United States showed great patience in the face of very considerable provocation. I remember

when we talked about this in the House of Commons last July 15. In my contribution to the debate on foreign affairs at that time I had this to say about Cuba and I have no cause to change the words used then. As found on page 6358 of Hansard, I said:
I think the United States of America has shown very great patience in this situation up to the present time against very considerable provocation. I suggest that the United States will have to show even more patience, and that is not going to be easy in the light of what is going on on the island of Cuba. Intervention by armed forces or intervention by forces of any kind, the illegal use of force to protect even vital economic and other interests, is not now possible in the world in which we live. The Suez incident certainly showed that, and the United States should be just about the first country in the world to draw the right conclusions from that incident.
What was the reason for this action? What should be done about it now? What should be the policy that we as neighbours of the United States should follow? What line should we take? It seems to me that the menace to the United States in the situation in Cuba is not a menace to her territorial integrity. That is nonsense. The United States could deal with Cuba in a few hours in a straight conflict between the two countries. The menace to the United States, and it is a very real one which we would certainly appreciate in this country if we were in a similar situation, is that Cuba may be used as a base for the extension of communism to other Latin American states by the centre of communist power, the Soviet union, exploiting for that purpose legitimate forces for economic and social progress in those countries and taking over those forces so that eventually they will become totalitarian satellites surrounding and pressing against the United States. This is the situation as a great many Americans see it; a communist base of that kind, not a menace to the United States directly, of course, but a menace in the way I have indicated; a base only 90 miles away from the shores of the United States, even closer than Formosa is to mainland China. Therefore American anxiety is understandable.
What should be done? I suggest not what was done last week where the worst of both worlds seems to have been achieved. I read yesterday an article from Washington written by Mr. Max Freedman who writes for the Manchester Guardian and the Winnipeg Free Press. He had this to say, and these are pretty worrying words:
The time has come to set down certain clear facts that have emerged from the wretched tangle of error and miscalculation that haunted the Cuban affair. The Kennedy administration intends to use force if necessary against the Castro government if no effective action can be obtained through the organization of American states.
External Affairs
Surely, Mr. Speaker, it is not inappropriate for a country that is her friend to urge the United States to bring about the appropriate action that is necessary through the organization of American states. Otherwise, it means unilateral intervention. The long range result of that, however great the provocation, would surely be unhappy in terms of relations between the United States and her Latin American colleagues in the organization of American states who have shown themselves over the years to be so sensitive about American unilateral intervention even when it was justified. It would also be an unhappy development for the position of the United States in the Atlantic coalition, even more so if the United States could be charged before the United Nations, however unfairly and unjustly, even on a technicality of aggression.
Therefore I can only express the hope, as I am sure all hon. members do, that whatever action may have to be taken will be taken collectively through the organization of American states or at least attempted through that organization.
The President himself made a statement on April 20. This is the one that has caused so much interest, not unmixed with anxiety. The President said this, and these are the words that have been quoted so much in Canadian newspapers in recent days:
Should it ever appear that the inter-American doctrine of non-interference merely conceals or excuses a policy of non-action-if the nations of this hemisphere should fail-
We are told he did not mean Canada.
-to meet their commitments against outside communist penetration-then I want it clearly understood that this government will not hesitate in meeting its primary obligations which are to the security of our own nation.
I interpret this to mean that if there is outside aggression against a Latin American state or against the United States, the United States will discharge its obligations for assistance and for its own security, under the appropriate treaty. I get some support for that interpretation from the first sentence of that same paragraph of the President's statement which has not been quoted very much. He said this-these are good words:
Any unilateral American intervention, in the absence of an external attack upon ourselves or an ally, would have been contrary to our traditions and to our international obligations.
I should like to think that is still the policy of the United States government. In other words, intervention will be based on collective resistance to aggression under the appropriate hemisphere doctrine. That doctrine, of course, is the Monroe doctrine which goes back to 1823. We have been told at school that this doctrine should really be called the "Canning's policy" because if it had not

External Affairs
been for George Canning and the British navy President Monroe would never have been able to put it into effect early in the 19th century. President Monroe enumerated it in 1823. It is interesting to read his words now. All you have to do is change a couple of words and his statement is applicable to the situation today. He said, in 1823:
It was impossible that the allied powers should extend their political system to any portion of either (American) continent without endangering our peace and happiness; nor can anyone believe that our southern brethren-
The Latin American states.
-if left to themselves, would adopt it of their own accord.
That has a 1961 ring. This doctrine has been interpreted in various ways throughout the century. The recognized American interpretation, and the one on which the United States government has acted in recent years was laid down by secretary of state Olney in the latter part of the 19th century when he said -I hope it is still this interpretation of the Monroe doctrine which will prevail:
It does not justify any attempt on our part to change the established form of government or any American state or to prevent the people of such state from altering that form according to their will and pleasure.
The latest statement bearing on this doctrine was made at the inter-American conference at Caracas in 1954. 1 think it is interesting to put on the record now a paragraph from that declaration. It certainly has a bearing on this situation and, I venture to hope, will guide the policy of the United States government when it faces difficult problems in the days ahead. The United States and the Latin American states in 1954 accepted this declaration:
That the domination or control of the political institutions of any American state by the international communist movement, extending to this hemisphere the political system of an extracontinental power, would constitute a threat to the sovereignty and political independence of the American states, endangering the peace of America, and would call for a meeting of consultation to consider the adoption of appropriate action in accordance with existing treaties.
This would seem to me, Mr. Speaker, to give any member of the organization of American states adequate power to invoke collective action in the situation set out in that paragraph, that is one of communist aggression against or domination of American states. Section III of this declaration states:
This declaration of foreign policy made by the American republics in relation to dangers originating outside this hemisphere is designed to protect and not to impair the inalienable right of each American state freely to choose its own form of government and economic system and to live its own social and cultural life.
I cannot help but think that if the United States government took unilateral action- I am not suggesting it will-against the provisions of that particular paragraph there might be a difficult situation created, especially in view of what secretary Herter had to say at the Santiago conference in 1959. This also has a bearing on the present situation. He had been talking about intervention and non-intervention and relating it to the earlier Caracas conference. Secretary Herter said:
Moreover, it appears that at least some of these expeditions were organized in other countries with the knowledge and consent of officials whose governments were pledged to prevent such action. Expeditions have obtained arms from official sources in other countries despite public declarations of policy to the contrary.
Some of these movements have been justified before the public on the grounds that they were undertaken for the purpose of establishing more democratic regimes in certain countries and that thereby they helped to fulfil a principle of the charter of the O.A.S.
I do not wish to speculate on what the motives may have been behind these interventionist activities. Yet, whether or not they were commendable we cannot conduct our inter-American relations on the theory that the end justifies the means, and that the charter and other treaties may be flouted at will.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, the United States government will adopt this attitude toward the problem about which we have been talking, and I am sure that by adopting such an attitude they will get the other American states behind them, thereby enabling them to take stronger action against communist penetration than would be possible by any form of unilateral action. That is what we must have in mind in our own country because we recognize today the provocation and menace in what is happening in Cuba. We hope that this menace can be dealt with in a way that will not make it difficult for the friends of the United States who ask for nothing better than to follow her wise leadership in the search for peace and security in the world.
I talk like this tonight as a Canadian. But Canada is not in the organization of American states. We are told that President Kennedy did not have Canada in mind when he talked about the western hemisphere. I am sure he was thinking only about the members of that organization. It seems to me that if we are to recognize this new-it is at least new in its manifestations-menace of communist penetration, this use of a Latin American state as a base for communist penetration into other American states, this taking advantage of a legitimate desire for economic and social change which cannot and should not be damned; if we feel that the menace can best be dealt with by collective action
[Mr. Pearson.1

through the organization of American states, and if it is a menace to Canada as much as to any other state in the western hemisphere, then perhaps the time has some for Canada to take its responsibilities as a member of the organization of American states. Perhaps we should not wait for the Canadian institute of international affairs to tell us what to do in this regard in view of this changed situation; although, I am sure the minister will get the best advice in the world from the public-spirited experts of that institute.
So I should like to echo what the hon. member for Essex East said yesterday. In view of the growing importance of Latin America in the world; its economic and commercial importance; in view of the necessity of the states of the western hemisphere working together to deal with these dangers of communist penetration, sympathetic consideration should be given by the minister now to something which he seemed to be considering very sympathetically a year or so ago, the problem of Canadian association with the organization of American states. That is one piece of advice, and I think it is the only piece of advice I have given to the minister, in a speech which is already far too long.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the concluding minutes of this very important debate, I merely wish to speak very briefly on Canada and the Pacific. I shall confine myself to this topic for three reasons. The first reason is that as a member of NATO we agree with the principle of the need to help undeveloped countries and these undeveloped countries are situated mainly in Africa and Asia. The second reason is that we also have member commonwealth countries in the Pacific. My last reason for talking about Canada and the Pacific is that we shall have to consider the competition between the free world and the communist bloc to win those uncommitted countries, and our discussions will underline the fact that the problems facing us are changing from month to month and that we must use great imagination to solve these problems.
In our dealings with other nations, Mr. Speaker, and in our effort to find solutions to the various political and economic problems, I suggest that we must first reassess our own thinking in order to find out if some of the things in which we believed some 50 years, 25 years or 10 years ago are still valid. I particularly have in mind the concept of the sovereignty of nations. My concept of the sovereignty of nations is that each country has the right to administer its domestic affairs without interference from other countries.
A few years ago I suppose that if a country had sufficient natural resources, a large
90205-6-258
External Affairs
population and an economy sufficiently developed to supply the needs of its own people from its own resources and if this country had reasonably capable leaders, this concept might hold true. But is this concept true today, Mr. Speaker? Can any country stand alone sufficient unto itself? Using my earlier criteria I can think of only two great powers which come near to fulfilling these qualifications and these great powers are the United States of America and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics; and even these two great powers are dependent on other countries for many vital things.
It appears to me, Mr. Speaker, that many countries in the free world have recognized that national sovereignty is a highly effective rallying cry for domestic politics, but in international dealings a rigid adherence to the concept of national sovereignty is unrealistic. It is for this very reason that 15 nations have joined themselves into NATO. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has said, "There is no sovereignty without survival".
I know that many Canadians feel strongly about sovereignty. There has been criticism that we are a satellite of the United States and that our armed forces are but mere appendages to the U.S. forces and therefore subject to the whim of the Pentagon in Washington.
Let us be realistic, Mr. Speaker. No matter how much it may appeal to us in our hearts and to our national pride can we, by virtue of our physical limitations, stand by ourselves in trying to solve our problems of defence and of trade? On the other hand, in spite of these physical limitations, Canada's role in international affairs is such that we are being regarded more and more as a major power. I suggest that Canada is living proof that a country need not have huge armed forces in order to be considered a major influence in world affairs.
We can therefore see that the concept of national sovereignty is altering because in NATO, by voluntarily sacrificing some of our sovereignty, we preserve our right to survive. Survival then, in modern times, is based on a collective arrangement. This implies a sharing with other nations not only of obligations but also of benefits; and this brings me to the subject of trade and assistance to the underdeveloped countries of the world and to the topic on which the minister himself spoke at length, namely, Canada and the Pacific.
On November 2, 1959, Mr. Paul-Henri Spaak, who was then secretary general of

External Affairs
NATO, addressed the Imperial defence college in London. Among other things this is what he said:
Provided that the military forces in the free world are maintained efficient and up to date, it may well he that Europe will no longer be the main scene of the long term struggle between communism and the free world. This will very largely take place in the economically underdeveloped countries of Africa and Asia.
His statement was followed in December by the Atlantic congress of NATO which reiterated the need to switch the emphasis from military forces to economic co-operation not only among the NATO countries themselves but also in the underdeveloped areas of the world. On November 11, 1957, 1 myself spoke in the House of Commons about the aspect of aid to the underdeveloped countries. Because of the shortness of time at my disposal I will not make detailed reference to or quote my own speech.
Mr. Speaker, we can be proud of our contribution to some of these countries. The assistance which we have extended under the Colombo plan has been far-reaching, ably administered and well received. If anything, we have been unduly modest in letting others know about our contribution. However, not all of the contributions of the free world to these underdeveloped countries have had the same results. There have been cases of extravagance and poor administration and, instead of earning good will and friendship, we have in some instances suffered ridicule and animosity.
In our haste to woo the uncommitted countries, we have sometimes poured money into projects which at best are of a stop-gap nature and which cannot produce lasting results. Measures designed as emergency help catch us on the horns of our own dilemma because if we were to discontinue this type of help the U.S.S.R. would step in to fill the vacuum. Yet we dare not impose control or restrictions because to direct that long range measures must be undertaken by the recipients in order to help develop industry, promote education, social welfare and the like, would leave us open to the charge that we are interfering in domestic matters.
We must therefore revise our thinking in so far as financial aid to these countries is concerned. Financial aid alone is not enough. That help must be extended with a genuine and sympathetic interest. We have heard reports to the effect that loan administrators have gone into countries and that the first thing they did was to set up a private club for their social life. There is nothing wrong with that procedure because anyone going to

a strange country instinctively turns to something familiar. But let us contrast this procedure with the actions of the communist mayor of the city of Semarang in Indonesia, who works twice a week for a total of seven hours "for free" in order to help construct village roads and schools. He has also collected from the sale of empty bottles, enough money to build a primary school.
In competing to win the friendship of the people in these underdeveloped and uncommitted countries we sometimes forget to take into account their temperament, background and philosophy. Because they experiment with communism we are afraid that they will turn communist. Let us not forget that, in the eyes of these people, neither the communists nor the people of the free world approach them with spotless records. To these countries the great attraction of communism is that, under a socialist system, the U.S.S.R. has been able in a very short time to catch up with and in certain areas to surpass the west.
Let us remember that many of the Asiatic peoples have developed over a long, long time their own philosophies and cultures and that to them communism is something which appears to be another philosophy which they can examine and with which they can experiment without any danger of losing their basic philosophy. A recent example of this is the overthrow of the communist government in the state of Karala in India. These Asian people are a patient people and they are prepared to wait 10 years, 50 years or 100 years for their television sets or homes with two-car garages. However, there is no doubt that they want their independence now; and it is in this respect that they are impatient because they feel that independence will give them dignity.
To a people who were creative and artistic enough to be wearing silks and to have developed a very sophisticated culture when some of our forefathers were still roaming the country in animal skins, time is not measured in generations but in hundreds of centuries. That is why spiritual and personal dignity mean more to these people than next year's car.
Mr. Speaker, Canada's role in the Pacific is a significant one. We have had a good start with the Colombo plan. But Canada must also look to its own expansion. New expansion means more trade, but where are we going to get this trade? Even within the commonwealth we do have the trade that we would like.
In an effort to establish economic stability and to encourage economic expansion nations are now forming economic blocs without too much regard for political implications. It may

well be that the establishment of the European common market marks the beginning of a new era in world trade, because nations are beginning to enter into economic alliances even where they differ geographically, politically and racially.
I suggest that an example of this is Australia. Drawn by her political and racial background to the west, she is in a natural and physical position to contribute a great deal to Africa and Asia, much more so than Canada. When the time comes, is Australia to sacrifice a magnificent opportunity purely in the name of the commonwealth, and insist on trading with only the English speaking nations of the world? I think not. For that same reason I suggest that Canadians take a new look at our relations with our neighbour the U.S.A. and every other country in the world.
In the economic battle ahead we must use every bit of ingenuity, strive for maximum efficiency and make bold moves because we are facing ruthless competition. As Mr. Khrushchev said as far back as 1955 to a group of visiting United States congressmen:
We value trade least for economic reasons and most for political reasons.
Recent events have shown no changes in the position taken by Mr. Khrushchev. That is why I am glad to hear the minister say that he intends to pay more attention to the Latin American countries.
Finally, may I say a word about the efforts of the minister to bring about discussions on disarmament. At the United Nations he has established himself as a man dedicated to peace. To those who know him, this is not surprising. However, his efforts at the United Nations have not all been warmly received and I know there must have been times when the minister felt discouraged. But it is the mark of a man, Mr. Speaker, that in spite of these difficulties he has persisted in his efforts.
The fact that Canada was a member of the ten power disarmament committee is eloquent testimony to the work done by the minister, and I give him my wholehearted support in anything that he does which will bring about fruitful discussions.
I put on record my support for his efforts for disarmament, because there are some in this country who seem to think that our leaders are uninformed and indifferent to the consequences of a nuclear conflict.
Those who hold that attitude, in my opinion, do a great disservice to the people of Canada when they try to spread the picture of our leaders callously leading our country to destruction. No one knows better than the Prime Minister, the minister himself, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness), 90205-6-258i
External Affairs
and others in the government, the horrors of nuclear war. Most of us in this chamber have served our country in war and no one need lecture us as to the waste and futility of war.
The mere fact that we are maintaining our defence until such time as a satisfactory formula for disarmament is found is entirely consistent with government policy. Indeed, how can anyone, in all honesty, advocate unilateral disarmament on our part when there is no similar desire on the part of others?
Disarmament could be accomplished tomorrow if the major nuclear powers could agree to the necessary procedures for inspection. But until such time we can only support the efforts of the minister in trying to bring together the nuclear powers so that disarmament discussions may be continued.
Learning how to live together is much more difficult than learning how to fight together. There are times when we will be impatient, but we cannot all at once build for a hundred years. None the less, I am in agreement with the statement made last year by the minister when he said that Canada will end this decade as one of the leading nations of the world.
When we achieve that status-and I say this without derogating in any way from the contributions made by his colleagues or predecessors in office-I am sure that the minister will derive great personal satisfaction from the contribution he has made in helping Canada attain that position.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that under the rules I have no right of reply in this debate. However, perhaps hon. members of the house will bear with me for a minute while I express to those who have participated in the discussion-as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) so aptly called it a few moments ago-my thanks for the manner in which the debate has been conducted, and also for the very helpful suggestions which have been made.
Quite a few hon. members had hoped to participate in this debate but have not been able to do so because we allotted just two days for it. Of course, I was personally responsible for several hon. members being unable to take part because I spoke too long yesterday afternoon. For that I apologize.
However, I understand that the sittings of the external affairs committee are to commence next week and I plan to be available for interrogation, further suggestions and criticisms in that committee before leaving for the NATO meeting in Oslo a week from tomorrow night.

Business of the House
I am sure we can all look forward to further consideration of these vital foreign affairs problems and that this consideration will be a great help to our own nation, as I feel this debate has been during the last two days.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Pursuant to the order of the house made on Tuesday last, it is now my duty to put the question on the motion now before the house. Before doing so I may say that the special order of the house was probably wide enough, as it permitted a general debate, to permit the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) to make his last intervention. However, that does not fall to be decided now.
Accordingly, the question is the following:
Mr. Green moves that items Nos. 76 to 110 inclusive and item No. 481 as listed in the main estimates 1961-62 referring to the Department of External Affairs, be withdrawn from the committee of supply and referred to the standing committee on external affairs, saving always the powers of the committee of supply in relation to the voting of public moneys.
Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I inquire what the program is for tomorrow and next week.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Tomorrow, the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce. The suggested program for next week will run as
follows. The first item on Monday will be No. 6 on today's order paper, Bill No. C-85 referring to the national design council.
The second item will be the resolution in the name of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys dealing with the Coal Production Assistance Act. The third item will be the resolution in my name dealing with the army benevolent fund. These two resolutions will perhaps not take up much time of the house.
The fourth item will be Bill No. C-84, which is item No. 5 on today's order paper, an act respecting the vocational rehabilitation of disabled persons, etc. On the order paper tomorrow I expect there will appear a bill dealing with amendments to the Fisheries Act. This will then be available as a fifth item. I am speaking now of Monday and Tuesday combined.
If time permits, we may finally reach Bill No. C-77, which is item No. 4 on today's order paper, dealing with agricultural development.
The intention at the moment is to proceed on Wednesday, Thursday, Friday and Saturday with the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and, if good progress is made, perhaps the estimates of a third department will be made available for discussion on Saturday. I will announce that later.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
